title: Founder Legal Radar
question: How can a startup founder identify legal issues that need attention and keep track of the next decision?
expression: A selected register of United States startup legal issues, with an official source and source type for each record. Founders can filter by business profile and product exposure, move records through unreviewed, watching, ask counsel and closed states, save their review, and export it as JSON. The purpose is to turn a reading list into a manageable review process.
boundary: Deliberately selected rather than comprehensive, and educational issue spotting only. It is not legal advice, creates no attorney-client relationship, and the register does not attempt to cover every exposure a company may have.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: DEA Scheduling Monitor
question: How can researchers find significant DEA actions without reading every routine notice?
expression: The documented monitor collects Drug Enforcement Administration documents from the Federal Register over a rolling 180-day window. It separates final rules, proposals open for comment, quotas and temporary orders from registrations and general notices. Its views use the same underlying document set, and a source-health panel reports refresh status.
boundary: This is document discovery, not legal interpretation. Classification does not establish how a document applies to a substance, registrant or programme. Collection dates and source health must be checked before treating the feed as current.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: NSAG Lead Intelligence
question: How can the Neurocognitive Systems Advisory Group see enquiries from its different modules in one place?
expression: An internal dashboard designed to combine module enquiries, filter them by module and organisation tier, show summary totals, and export records as CSV. It belongs to the advisory practice’s administrative work rather than its public research collection.
boundary: The dashboard and enquiry data are private and access-restricted. Assessment collection is paused across the related programme; this description does not establish an active intake service, current enquiry volume or a completed privacy and security audit.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: AI Governance Tracker
question: How can someone track AI-related enforcement, legislation and professional guidance without confusing discovery with verified authority?
expression: The documented collector groups search results into FTC enforcement, state and federal legislation, bar ethics, ABA guidance and EU AI Act coverage. It is configured for Monday sweeps and exposes a dashboard and JSON feed. Collection-health fields report the last sweep, record age, failed searches, newest item and a stale flag after two missed cycles.
boundary: Search results include both primary documents and secondary reporting. Collection is not verification or legal analysis. The schedule describes the implementation; it does not certify that the latest scheduled run succeeded.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: Legal AI Guidance Monitor
question: How can legal practitioners distinguish an actual AI-related opinion or court order from commentary about it?
expression: A source register separates reviewed authorities from newly discovered candidates. The recorded review covered ABA Formal Opinion 512, four state or city bar opinions, two Middle District of Florida standing orders and one Ninth Circuit sanctions opinion. Each record identifies jurisdiction, authority type, review date and official source. A separate discovery process can add candidates without automatically treating them as verified.
boundary: The existing portfolio record dates the eight-authority review to August 17, 2026 and reports a stale discovery sweep last completed August 10. Those are historical checks, not assurance of current legal coverage. Authorities require renewed review before reliance; this is not legal advice.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: Psych Ops Source Watch

expression: A documented weekly source monitor covers six official endpoints, including Oregon and Colorado programme sources. It screens discovered links against a source policy and reports category status, healthy or failed sources, and the age of the last successful sweep. Its purpose is to build a review queue that a person can inspect.
boundary: A screened link is still an unreviewed lead. A registered endpoint does not prove a new rule was issued or that a recent sweep succeeded. The monitor does not interpret law or verify clinical claims.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: Platform Moderation Evidence Lab

boundary: An individual reversal does not establish a platform-wide pattern, motive or legal violation. The collection covers selected public records, and visitor priority flags are review choices rather than findings.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: Culture Intelligence Monitor

boundary: The consumer-behaviour interpretations are hypotheses. Neither demand predictions nor the risk score have been validated, and the prototype does not establish campaign results.

title: Drug Market Transition Evidence Lab

The contribution is a structured evidence record rather than a new empirical study.
boundary: It organises published evidence. It does not generate findings, and an absence of evidence in a dimension is recorded as an absence rather than as a null result.
provenance: Existing portfolio record; catalogued October 2026.

title: Entheogen Atlas

Contested ancient-use claims are kept distinct from claims supported by chemical analysis.
boundary: The atlas is a documented research build. Its historical and scientific claims have not received a complete independent review in this gallery audit. No universal earliest-use date, clinical benefit or endorsement of use is established here.

title: Microdosing Knowledge Atlas

boundary: A catalogue of references, not a reproduction of the works or an authorised archive. Link checks describe access at a recorded time; they do not verify the source’s scientific claims or guarantee that a link still works.

title: AI Build Cost Workbench

boundary: Outputs are the user's own planning scenarios. They are not quotes, and they are not independently validated market benchmarks.

title: Source Integrity Workbench

boundary: The score measures documentation completeness, not truth and not source authentication. Legal, clinical, scientific and regulatory conclusions still need the appropriate qualified reviewer.

boundary: A planning tool, not a certification and not an autonomous operating system.

title: Herbal Histories
question: What happens when a familiar story about a psychoactive plant is checked against the documents it is supposed to rest on?
expression: A Polymath historical series investigating claims about psychoactive plants through statutes, newspapers, manuscripts and other records. Its method compares the original wording with later retellings, identifies translation choices and separates direct evidence from inference. The broader cultural-activation framework connects plant knowledge with communities, trade, research and regulation. The Windbreak Decree provides a published example: a document-based investigation of Dutch cannabis-law history and the stories told about its origins. Imagine This Same Vice Squad offers a second published example, reading newspaper coverage of Louis Armstrong alongside reporting on unequal enforcement and separating the article’s interpretation from the newspaper’s own statements. Added to Chapter examines a San Francisco opium ordinance and its supporting claim ledger. A Hundred Pounds an Acre follows Trinidad’s cultivation, prohibition and licensing rules while keeping colonial testimony and missing records visible. Ganga (Cannabis Sativa) examines Jamaica’s 1913 legislation and the evidence behind accounts of cannabis arriving and spreading on the island. Suggested but Not Proven follows a claim about Shakespeare across literary interpretation, residue analysis, archaeological context and press coverage. The Qualities of Native Medicines follows clinical cases, collaborators and changing editions of a nineteenth-century Indian hemp paper. The Ropes in the Pyramid of Unas examines how an uncertain Egyptian plant-word became a confident modern identification and records the limits of that argument. Free Access to the Tree of Life compares Rastafari founding texts, Jamaican statutes and later testimony, with a supporting statute exhibit. Nor Cause the Indians to Take Them examines the Mexican Inquisition’s peyote edict, its jurisdiction and the limits of the surviving case record. The Soma That No One Drinks follows attempts to identify a ritual plant through hymns, substitution rules, translation choices and unresolved archaeological evidence. The Experiments Were All Made on Myself compares Arthur Heffter’s account of his research with earlier reports to ask what the Leipzig experiments actually established. I Have Seen It Nowhere But Egypt compares Avicenna’s hemp entries with a botanist’s eyewitness account and traces how later writers used that account. The Theatrical Takings Were Thin traces the Paris club legend through theatre writing, medical accounts and letters. Nobody Took the Children to Find God compares accounts of a Mazatec vigil with what later publications made of it. Five Kingdoms of Plants distinguishes the words of an Atharvaveda hymn from later translations and a modern botanical identification. Siddhi as Prasad compares testimony about offerings at Baidyanath with the commission’s final account of religious custom and licensed trade. Be Careful How You Use It follows the registration warning in a wartime hemp film through contracts, crop statistics and the film catalogs in which it appeared. Seeing Ghosts and Running About follows a Chinese hemp passage through competing editions, disputed plant-part readings and the later claims made from it. The Midwife Who Was Not There follows a medieval-childbirth claim through plant remedies, witch-hunt writing and later retellings, alongside a draft companion about checking health stories. He Wrote One Paragraph separates Herodotus’s account from two distant excavations and the later interpretations connecting them. The College Anslinger Never Graduated From examines an archive's filing categories and the limits of reasoning from unopened folders, alongside a draft companion about a Senate hearing.
boundary: The series has verified published writing, so it is more than a proposal. This review confirms twenty-two essays’ current publication and complete texts; it does not certify the full twenty-five-issue scope described in the series introduction, every translation, or a complete multimedia collection. Traditional use is not clinical evidence. Historical and legal claims, cultural authority and reuse rights still require work-level review.

title: Imagine This Same Vice Squad
question: What does contemporary Black newspaper coverage reveal about Louis Armstrong’s cannabis prosecution, unequal enforcement and the limits of the story later retellings preserve?
expression: A published Herbal Histories essay closely reading two March 1931 California Eagle front pages and a later Associated Negro Press report. It distinguishes Armstrong’s reported sentence and parole from an arrest narrative that the consulted newspaper does not establish. Its broader argument concerns how police and court reporting shape which parts of a person’s life enter the archive. In a later draft companion, RN puts the newspaper account beside historical military reports from the Panama Canal Zone. She distinguishes what police and journalists recorded from what military investigators set out to measure.

question: What can the wording, compilation history and enforcement records of a San Francisco opium ordinance establish about the familiar story of America’s first drug law?
expression: A published Herbal Histories essay comparing a municipal code’s dated credit line with later accounts of when an opium ordinance began. It distinguishes the date a provision entered a compiled chapter from the possibility of an earlier enactment, and compares restrictions on trade with restrictions on premises and visitors. The essay reads enforcement tables alongside other municipal measures, examining how apparently general legal language operated within an anti-Chinese political campaign. Its separately published supporting appendix supplies a chronology and a twenty-six-item claim ledger. Together they distinguish documents, attributed reports, interpretation and unresolved questions; the appendix supports the same investigation rather than constituting a second portfolio work. In a narrower draft companion, RN compares an 1882 physician’s claims and a historian’s account of public alarm with municipal records of rooms, charges and dismissals. She asks which claims those records could actually test.
boundary: Both current publication records and complete texts were reviewed. The essay and appendix leave the original proceedings and relevant daily press unexamined, so the codification date does not prove that no earlier ordinance existed. Their enforcement counts concern charges, not necessarily distinct people, and do not establish ancestry. A chronology inconsistency remains in both: an 1881 account is described as seven years into the ordinance’s life despite the central 1878 dating argument. This review does not resolve that discrepancy or independently verify the underlying documents, transcriptions, comparative legal claims, diagram or media rights. The complete texts remain on Polymath; no finished multimedia package is inferred. The later companion is a held draft. Its account of the 1878 addition does not settle the possibility of an earlier ordinance, the Board’s motives or any clinical effect. The public essay and appendix remain available separately below; the companion has no reading link.
provenance: Existing editorial catalogue’s essay–appendix relationship confirmed against current publisher metadata and both complete texts on November 3, 2026. One investigation with a supporting publication; source limitations and internal chronology issue retained. The complete companion and its AaN owner record were reviewed November 6, 2026. Any separate publication or video adaptation remains RN’s decision.

title: When Does One Person Become an Institution?
question: What distinguishes a person’s visibility or job title from durable capacity that can survive a change of employer, platform or role?
expression: The opening Institutions of One essay introduces RN’s Build, Carry, Control and Continue framework. It asks what a person has created, which capabilities and relationships can travel, who holds decision-making authority, and what can persist when an essential dependency changes. Six public cases contrast independent operators, creators, executives and public-sector work, avoiding the assumption that founding or owning a company is the only way to build institutional capacity. The essay brings business statistics, organizational theory, legal structures and succession research into a discussion of how to investigate those questions. Its contribution is a set of distinctions and an evidence-aware research method, not a ranking of the people discussed.
boundary: Current publisher metadata and the complete essay were reviewed. The article describes its Observatory as a methodology pilot, not a validated score or certification. Public announcements and first-person accounts do not establish private ownership, contract rights, governance or the ability to survive a dispute; no private contracts, ownership records or participant interviews were reviewed for the edition. Its applications of organizational theory and findings from other populations are interpretations with stated limits. This portfolio review does not independently verify the legal, statistical or historical claims, images or reuse rights, nor establish a completed media package.
provenance: Existing editorial catalogue reconciled with current publisher metadata and the complete opening essay on November 4, 2026. One published work within Institutions of One; the programme and its website remain separate related records.

title: Law Happens Somewhere — opening essay
question: How do the rooms, forms, timelines, resources and interactions surrounding a legal process determine whether people can actually participate?
expression: A published essay introducing RN’s developing Salutogenic Legal Design framework through everyday encounters with legal institutions. It maps eight overlapping sets of conditions, from legal authority and organizational decisions to resources, timing, communication, technology, physical settings and interpersonal treatment. The essay explains why RN retired an earlier three-part model and replaced it with six separate questions about intelligibility, resource responsibility, supported action, contestability, recognition and institutional response. A separate justice review asks whether redesign would improve access or merely make an unjust demand easier to enforce. Hypothetical examples illustrate the approach; the essay argues that changing or removing a demand may matter more than improving an interface.
boundary: Current publisher metadata and the complete essay were reviewed. This is published writing about an emerging research framework, not a validated assessment, composite score, clinical measure or demonstrated intervention. The essay explicitly rejects inferring a person’s nervous-system state from a setting or observed behavior and does not treat calm, efficiency or compliance as proof of justice. Legal examples and source references have not been independently rechecked in this portfolio review, and the photographs and diagram have not received visual or rights verification. The opening essay is an individual work within the series; it does not establish completion or review of every instalment.
provenance: Existing editorial catalogue reconciled with the current publisher record and complete opening essay on November 4, 2026. The published text identifies Law Happens Somewhere within Nervous System Aware Governance and updates the earlier registry-only description.

title: A Hundred Pounds an Acre
question: What do the surviving records show about Trinidad’s ganja laws, and how did the rules distinguish growing the plant from buying and selling it?
expression: RN Collins’s published Herbal Histories essay examines a frequently repeated account of Trinidad’s drug laws through colonial reports, ordinance tables, consolidated legislation, guidebooks and customs records. For readers interested in how plant histories and legal claims are constructed, it follows a reported cultivation fee, a later prohibition and a licensed trade through seven sections. RN compares the dates of events with the dates of the records describing them, explains the difference between repealing a law and creating exceptions to it, and examines officials’ accounts of labour and trade without treating those accounts as the labourers’ own testimony. An evidence-status section, an embedded chronology and a twenty-five-item claim ledger separate documentary findings, attributed reports, interpretations and unanswered questions. These appendices support this one investigation; the complete essay remains on Polymath.
boundary: Current publisher metadata identifies RN Collins as author and the essay as published, web-accessible and free; its complete text was reviewed for this description. The article does not establish that the 1885 measure was caused by the 1884 San Fernando killings. It reports that the enacted text of the 1885 ordinance, the original 1894 wording, relevant council debates and licence or prosecution series were not recovered. Its account of a later legal exception relies on a consolidated edition, and the proposed connection to Bengal remains an interpretation rather than documented legislative intent. Colonial claims about drug effects are attributed beliefs, not clinical evidence; the absence of growers’ voices is limited to the records consulted. This portfolio review has not independently verified the historical or legal claims, quotations, translations, diagrams, scan permissions or other media rights, and does not establish a completed multimedia package.
provenance: Existing editorial catalogue reconciled with current publisher metadata and the complete published essay, including both embedded appendices, on November 4, 2026. One writing record under Herbal Histories; no separate appendix work or new build.

title: Why Source Provenance Is Governance Infrastructure
question: How can an institution explain which evidence shaped a decision and find every affected use when that evidence changes?
expression: RN’s published essay for people who design, review or rely on institutional evidence records. Article six of Uncertainty Has an Owner, within Nervous System Aware Governance, begins with a hypothetical agency denial based on an AI summary whose citations conceal changes to the underlying evidence. RN distinguishes a source link from the longer record of how material was captured, changed, interpreted, reviewed and used. Her Provenance Spine connects eight steps: origin, capture, transformation, claim, review, decision, use and correction. A fourteen-field Decision Lineage Record turns that argument into a proposed working record, covering source versions and fragments, access restrictions, conflicting evidence, review authority, reasons for a decision, later reuse and responsibility for corrections. The essay compares citation, authentication, chain of custody, records management and data lineage; examines AI-assisted transformations; and offers an eight-question audit and a practical exercise tracing a claim backward to its source and forward to its consequences. Its minimum-sufficient-lineage principle asks for enough documentation to explain and repair consequential decisions while limiting collection, access and retention of sensitive information.
boundary: The essay is published; its proposed methods are not adopted standards, legal tests, empirically validated instruments or a demonstrated institutional deployment. Provenance records a claim’s history rather than proving it true. The agency scenario is hypothetical. The published text still calls for specialist review and testing the fourteen-field record on a public or owned workflow; this review found no evidence that those requirements were completed. Current publisher metadata and the complete article text, including captions and disclosure sections, were reviewed for this description. Cited legal, scientific and technical claims, source images, licensing assertions and practical effectiveness were not independently verified. This entry represents the essay, not completion of the twelve-article series or permission to disclose restricted evidence.
provenance: Current publisher record and complete published text reviewed November 4, 2026; reconciled with the existing editorial catalogue. RN Collins is the credited author. Full writing remains at its Polymath destination.

title: Why Institutions Automate Existing Confusion
question: Which unresolved institutional decisions become defaults, thresholds and handoffs when a process is automated?
expression: RN’s published essay for policy, legal, operational and technical teams preparing to automate consequential work. Article two of Uncertainty Has an Owner, within Nervous System Aware Governance, argues that making a process executable can conceal decisions the institution has never settled. RN develops an ambiguity inheritance principle: software carries forward unresolved definitions, evidence rules, exceptions and decision rights unless someone deliberately addresses them. Five registers organize the inquiry around categories, evidence, rules, handoffs and authority. The essay examines Australia’s Robodebt inquiry and U.S. Medicaid and SNAP oversight reports alongside a general institutional scenario, distinguishing the documented cases from RN’s proposed analysis. Its pre-automation audit pairs each register with a controlling question, required evidence and a stop condition. Teams are asked to resolve, preserve, bound or escalate each material ambiguity, or refuse automation where necessary, and record who owns the choice and what could reopen it. An accompanying workflow exercise maps exceptions, transfer points and powers to decide, override, correct or pause. The argument allows for automation’s benefits while separating consistent execution from a justified decision.
boundary: Current publisher metadata confirms RN Collins as author and the essay as published, web-accessible and free. Its complete text, including captions, references and evidence-status section, was reviewed for this description. The ambiguity inheritance principle, five registers, five dispositions and audit are RN’s proposed analytical framework, not adopted legal standards, validated assessment instruments or evidence of a completed implementation. The article’s Robodebt analysis is specific to that Australian inquiry; its U.S. oversight examples do not establish that all automated benefits systems are unlawful or that automation necessarily worsens decisions. This portfolio review did not independently verify the reports, legal interpretations, statistics, quotations, image rights or effectiveness of the method. Related production-package and scheduled derivative records are not additional completed works or release approval. Full writing remains on Polymath; no protected workflow information is disclosed.
provenance: Current publisher record and complete published text reviewed November 4, 2026; reconciled with the existing editorial catalogue and related private package pointer. No source publication or derivative approval change.

title: Why Human Review Requires Authority, Context, and Time
question: What must an institution give a human reviewer so they can change a consequential decision rather than merely approve it?
expression: RN’s published essay for people designing, supervising or challenging AI-assisted institutional decisions. Article one of Uncertainty Has an Owner, within Nervous System Aware Governance, introduces her ACT test: authority to change what happens next, context to understand the evidence and governing rule, and protected time to investigate before preventable harm. A composite review scenario shows how one-click approvals, burdensome overrides and speed targets can make formal oversight ineffective. RN distinguishes decision authority, process authority and system authority; explains why useful context is different from indiscriminate disclosure; and proposes risk-sensitive queues, escalation routes and correction records. A comparison table identifies practical evidence and warning signs for each condition. A closing exercise asks readers to trace a public workflow, including affected-person input and what happens after an error is found. The essay draws bounded comparisons with AI governance, medical-device human factors, aviation safety and health-care reliability while keeping their different legal settings explicit.
boundary: Current publisher metadata identifies RN Collins as author and the essay as published, web-accessible and free. The complete current text, including captions, references and evidence-status section, was reviewed for this description. ACT and its three authority layers are RN’s proposed analytical framework, not adopted legal standards, validated assessment instruments or evidence of a completed implementation. The opening is a composite scenario, not a report about a named institution. EU AI Act references remain limited by the law’s scope and timetable; medical-device, aviation and health-care comparisons do not establish rules for every institutional workflow. This review did not independently verify legal or scientific claims, source editions, quotations, images, rights or practical effectiveness. The older related carousel is archived; historical approval does not approve a successor or revised text. Full writing remains on Polymath, and the exercise excludes protected personal, client and institutional information.
provenance: Current publisher record and complete published text reviewed November 4, 2026; metadata reconfirmed November 5 UTC. Reconciled with the existing editorial catalogue and archived derivative record. RN Collins is the credited author; full writing remains on Polymath.

title: Ganga (Cannabis Sativa)
question: What do Jamaica’s 1913 statute and the records around it establish about ganja, and where do familiar origin stories depend on inference?
expression: RN Collins’s published Herbal Histories essay investigates Jamaica’s early cannabis restrictions and the evidence behind accounts of how the plant and its use reached the island. For readers interested in colonial history, migration and the construction of legal narratives, RN compares the printed Opium Law of 1913 with customs returns, medical reports, botanical inventories, immigration records, newspaper accounts and later scholarship. The seven-section investigation follows the wording of the law, the history of Indian indenture, competing accounts of transmission and the difference between a practice and the surviving paper record. An evidence-status section, an embedded chronology and a twenty-five-item claim ledger distinguish direct readings, second-hand quotations, interpretations and unresolved questions. The appendices belong to this one essay; the complete investigation remains on Polymath.
boundary: Current publisher metadata confirms RN Collins as author and the essay as published, web-accessible and free; the complete text was reviewed for this description. The article’s negative findings concern specified digitised records and imperfect text searches, not proof that cannabis, imports or use never existed. Its account of the Legislative Council exchange comes through a later reprint of a newspaper report, and two other press passages are also cited at second hand. The proposed transfer from Indian labourers to Afro-Jamaicans remains an inference without a direct record located by the author; an earlier African route is neither established nor ruled out here. Reported pre-indenture botanical specimens and early prosecution patterns remain unresolved. This portfolio review has not independently verified the historical, legal, botanical or linguistic claims, quotations, translations, source images, sensitivity determinations or reuse rights. It does not certify a completed multimedia package.
provenance: Existing article-intake catalogue reconciled with current publisher metadata and all seven sections, the evidence-status section and both embedded appendices of the published essay on November 4, 2026 Hawaiʻi. One Writing record under Herbal Histories; embedded supporting material is not counted as additional work.

title: Suggested but Not Proven
question: How did a qualified residue finding become a confident story about Shakespeare, and what evidence would be needed to connect the two?
expression: RN Collins’s published Herbal Histories essay examines the claim that Shakespeare used cannabis by following the relationship between a reading of Sonnet 76, chemical analysis of twenty-four clay pipe fragments and later retellings. For readers interested in literary history, archaeology and science reporting, RN compares editions and dictionaries, early botanical texts, accounts of the New Place excavations, a pilot study’s abstract, later scientific correspondence and newspaper coverage. Eight sections trace how statements about a sample, a place and a person became joined, and how qualifications changed as the story circulated. A detailed evidence-status section distinguishes material the author read directly from abstracts, metadata and sources that could not be obtained. The complete essay remains on Polymath.
boundary: Current publisher metadata identifies RN Collins as author and the essay as published, web-accessible and free; its complete text was reviewed for this description. The author did not obtain the original 2001 chemistry paper in full, so detection limits and procedural or sediment controls remain unverified. Missing controls in the accessible account do not show that no controls were used or that the chemistry was wrong. Later excavation findings describe the site and do not individually date the twenty-four tested fragments; accession details, published sample photographs and independent dating remain unrecovered in the article. The 2025 correspondence is represented by landing-page metadata, and the Oxford chapter by its abstract. The essay does not establish Shakespeare’s personal drug use. This portfolio review has not independently verified the literary, archaeological, historical or chemical claims, source quotations, images or reuse rights, and does not certify a completed multimedia package.
provenance: Existing article-intake catalogue reconciled with current publisher metadata and the complete eight-section essay and evidence-status section on November 4, 2026 Hawaiʻi. title: Who Is a Playground Built For? Huis, a Play Space on Wheels
question: How can a play space include children with different mobility and sensory needs, and what evidence would show whether its design helps?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay examines Huis, a mobile play installation by Studio Kars en Boom with RAUM. Written for readers interested in childhood, disability and public-space design, it brings together the makers’ accounts of working with children and research on accessible play, sensory experiences and children’s choices. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing about the installation. The manuscript distinguishes reviews of existing studies from a local playground-accessibility audit, school-based research and a small handheld-device experiment. An added section traces the earlier Straatscherm project and asks what observation and children’s own accounts could reveal about places to rest within a play space.

title: Could You Read a Curtain With Your Fingertips?
question: What can research on touch and learning tell us about reading a code embedded in a textile?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses Svenja Bremen’s Tactile Notation as a starting point for explaining how people perceive fine detail through touch and learn tactile reading. The designer’s translucent silk curtains carry flocked and wooden marks in her own notation system. For readers interested in design and neuroscience, RN brings the exhibition listing into conversation with research on fingertip receptors, tactile acuity and Braille training. The manuscript separates functional brain-imaging findings from a later structural study of the same learners, discusses a small stimulation experiment, and follows what happened when some learners were retested after training ended. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing; she did not design the textile or conduct these studies.

The cited papers, quotations, imagery and reuse rights have not been independently cleared in this portfolio review. Related upload and manuscript records remain one work.

title: Does Seasonal Food Taste Better? Attention, Expectation and the Table
question: How might attention and expectation change a meal, and what would establish whether seasonal food itself tastes better?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses Nature at the Table, a plant-based lunch created by Studio Daniëlle Ooms for Dutch Design Week 2025, to examine how eating is shaped by attention, memory and expectation. For readers interested in food, design and neuroscience, RN connects the documented event with three research accounts: a review of attention and food intake, an early brain-imaging study of wine-price expectations, and a later experiment comparing price-cued and blind wine ratings. The manuscript explains the shared table, local vegetables and tableware made with restaurant waste, crediting the makers and partners. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing; she did not design the lunch or conduct the studies.

Primary scientific claims, quotations, images and reuse rights have not been independently cleared in this portfolio review. Related manuscript and upload records remain one work.

title: Can a Bowl of Soup Make You Feel Less Alone?
question: What does research on shared meals and comfort food actually show about belonging, and how far can it explain a designed soup-table experience?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay examines Re-charge #3, HuisKamerCollab’s Dutch Design Week installation inviting visitors to sit at a long table, share soup and slow down. For readers interested in social connection, food and design, it describes the makers’ table, soundscape, film, material staging and graphics through the event listing. RN then compares a UK survey of 2,000 adults with two small undergraduate experiments on comfort food and thoughts of relationships. The writing explains why an association between eating together and reported wellbeing does not establish causation, and why an effect found among people with particular food or attachment associations cannot automatically be applied to everyone. RN’s role is documentary research and explanatory writing, not installation design or conducting the studies.
boundary: A prepared essay draft, not a verified magazine publication, observed installation evaluation or completed media package. The manuscript’s event description is listing-based. Its survey cannot establish that shared meals cause greater connection; the experiments involved 111 and 110 undergraduates and tested different tasks. One involved consuming soup already regarded as comfort food; the other involved writing about comfort food after a relationship threat. Neither tests this installation, eating soup with strangers, overstimulation or the sound and smell of its setting. Visitor behaviour and outcomes remain open questions. The current owner date and manuscript date differ, and neither establishes publication. Scientific claims, quotations, imagery and reuse rights have not been independently cleared in this portfolio review. Upload and manuscript records remain one work.
provenance: Complete current manuscript and current Ask a Neuroscientist long-form owner record reviewed. The owner identifies a Fat Nugs Magazine draft. Related source versions are consolidated without reproducing the manuscript or unreviewed media.

title: How a Nose Reads a Smell: Odorant Receptors
question: How does the nose distinguish smells, and what can one receptor structure reveal about a much larger sensory system?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay explains smell for readers curious about everyday perception and neuroscience. It follows the discovery of a large family of receptor genes, the idea that smells activate combinations of receptors, and a 2023 study showing one human receptor bound to a molecule associated with cheese. RN connects that history with later work cataloguing intact receptor genes, broken copies and differences between people. The manuscript distinguishes mouse and human counts, explains why estimates vary, and separates a gene catalogue from evidence about which molecules a receptor detects. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing; she did not perform the genetic, imaging or cell experiments.
boundary: A prepared Fat Nugs Magazine column draft, not a verified publication or finished media package. The account of the 1999 coding study comes through Nobel summaries rather than a direct reading of that paper. Estimates of distinguishable smells differ across the cited sources. The structural study concerns one receptor in its active form; changes were tested in laboratory cells, and the proposed activation model is explicitly speculative. Gene counts and small tissue samples do not establish how every person experiences smell. No independent scientific, quotation, image or reuse-rights clearance is claimed by this portfolio review. Related upload and manuscript records are one work.
provenance: Complete manuscript review retained at the unchanged source revision and reconciled with the current Ask a Neuroscientist owner register. The owner identifies a Fat Nugs Magazine draft; current portfolio and Polymath title checks found no matching entry. No manuscript body or unreviewed media is reproduced.

title: Why Does Time Fly When You're Having Fun?
question: Why can an experience feel short while it happens and long in memory, and how does that differ from the feeling that time is passing quickly?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay explains three experiences that everyday language often mixes together: estimating duration while expecting to judge it, estimating duration afterward, and reporting how fast time seems to pass. For readers interested in attention, emotion and memory, RN compares attention-based timing models, a review of 117 experiments, a small daily-life study, accounts of motivation, a lockdown survey and a free-fall experiment. The manuscript follows how mental workload, remembered changes, mood and fear can lead to different answers depending on the question and study design. RN’s role is documentary research and explanatory writing, translating the distinctions and study limits without claiming to have conducted the research.
boundary: A prepared Fat Nugs Magazine column draft, not a verified publication, validated timing model or completed media package. The daily-life study involved 27 adults; the lockdown survey relied on volunteers and remembered ratings of earlier life, so neither establishes causation. The unavailable 2012 motivation paper is represented through a later review. Short laboratory tasks do not establish how weeks or holidays are experienced, and the cited holiday demonstration lacks a reported sample size in the account used. The free-fall result distinguishes recalled duration from digit-reading performance; its proposed brain explanation was speculative. Planned dates differ between the manuscript and current owner record. Scientific claims, quotations, imagery and reuse rights have not been independently cleared in this portfolio review. Upload and manuscript versions remain one work.
provenance: Complete manuscript review retained at the unchanged source revision and reconciled with the current Ask a Neuroscientist owner record. Draft status is established; differing planned dates do not establish publication. No full source text or unreviewed media is reproduced.

title: Who Designs the Route From GP to Hospital and Back?

RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing, connecting programme descriptions with published research while distinguishing a method’s intentions from measured outcomes. The manuscript expressly does not rely on attendance, and RN did not design the hospital’s care pathways or conduct the studies.

title: Art That Watches Back: Attention, Agency and an Artwork That Forgets

title: Who Were Psychedelic Trials Tested On, and Can the Results Apply to Everyone?
question: Who takes part in psychedelic clinical trials, and what does that mean for people who differ from the participants?
expression: RN’s draft science essay examines who participates in psychedelic therapy research and how that affects the interpretation of results. Written for readers of research and public policy, the revised manuscript moves from an FDA advisory meeting and agency correspondence to reviews of race, ethnicity, income and education reporting, then compares two later-stage MDMA trials. RN’s contribution is documentary research, synthesis and explanatory writing, not conducting the trials. The essay distinguishes enrolling a diverse sample from reporting participant characteristics and testing whether outcomes differ between groups. It explains how prior experience, expectations, unsuccessful blinding and participant dropouts complicate interpretation, and presents arguments that expectancy concerns may be overstated alongside their limitations. The recovered output includes the long-form manuscript, references, resource links and proposed documentary and chart illustrations. It remains a science companion to RN’s civil-rights column.

title: After the Session: What Brain and Body Studies Show About the Weeks That Follow
question: What do studies actually measure in the days and weeks after a psychedelic session, and what remains unknown about aftercare?
expression: RN’s prepared Polymath science essay examines the period after a psychedelic experience for readers trying to distinguish research findings from broad claims about brain change. RN compares animal studies of social learning and neuronal structure, a survey of people reporting lasting difficulties, definitions of integration and a review of how treatment and safety outcomes are measured. The essay organizes findings by species, study design and what was actually observed. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing, not conducting the studies or providing treatment. It was prepared as a science companion to RN’s separate duty-of-care essay, connecting a question about responsibility with the limits of the available evidence.

title: How Often Do You Pick Up Your Phone Without Noticing?
question: What can research tell us about unnoticed phone checks and attempts to change social-media habits?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses Uitgescrolled, Noortje van Velzen’s social-media repair café, to examine the gap between how people remember using phones and what usage logs record. Written for readers interested in attention and everyday media habits, it follows the exhibition’s four steps: noticing habits, weighing benefits and costs, choosing a challenge and continuing the discussion at home. RN compares a small phone-logging study, a short randomized digital-media restriction trial, a meta-analysis and research on posting habits, attention, body comparison and family discussion. The output is an explanatory manuscript linking a design question to the different questions each study can answer. RN researched and wrote the essay; she did not design the exhibition or conduct the cited studies.

title: How Do You Track a Moving Ball Without Seeing It?
question: How do hearing, head movement, training and the social setting shape participation in ball sports without sight?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay starts with Visioball, described in the Fontys Dutch Design Week listings as a ball for visually impaired children. For readers interested in accessible design and perception, RN compares research on blind footballers trapping a sounding ball, laboratory sound localization and visually impaired students’ experiences of physical education. The manuscript separates a possible sensory mechanism from the wider question of inclusion, and briefly examines climate-image and restorative-room research alongside other Fontys exhibits. RN’s contribution is documentary research and explanatory writing that identifies what designers would still need to demonstrate. She did not create Visioball, test its mechanism or conduct the cited research.

title: Why Does a Gentle Stroke Feel Good?

expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column connects two Dutch Design Week projects, Plura Studio’s Touch On Connection and Katrijn Westland’s Soft Companions, with research on how people experience gentle touch. title: How Close Is Too Close? Personal Space, the Amygdala and a Room That Listens

expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column introduces Proximate Intimacies, Laura Papke’s installation made with Harm Belt, through its published exhibition listing. title: A Room Built for Silence: What Quiet Might Do to a Brain
question: What can research on silence and environmental noise tell us about a designed listening room—and what remains untested?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column uses the 2025 Dutch Design Week archive account of HuisKamerCollab’s Re-charge #2 to explore quiet, attentive listening and brain research. It introduces the credited collective’s hanging quilts, soundscape, objects and speakers, then explains a mouse experiment on auditory exposure, a review of traffic noise and mental health, and a conceptual proposal about built environments. RN’s role is documentary research, synthesis and explanatory writing; the room and its components are the makers’ work, and attendance is not established.

title: Is "Hangry" Real? What Hunger Does to Mood
question: How does hunger relate to anger and irritability, and how well do the familiar explanations fit the evidence?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column explains the everyday experience of feeling irritable before eating. For general readers, it connects interoception with a 21-day study of self-reported hunger and mood, laboratory work on emotional context, disputed glucose and self-control explanations, and mouse research on feeding circuits and territorial aggression. The manuscript describes study designs, separates associations from explanations, distinguishes statistical models and identifies where findings cannot transfer across species. RN’s evidenced role is research synthesis and explanatory writing, rather than conducting these experiments. The supporting package contains a nine-slide sequence, platform adaptations, interview prompts, chart and figure specifications, a short video script and a longer narrated adaptation. These are prepared materials; the scripts do not establish that filming or publication occurred.

title: Can a Surface Calm You Down? On Touch and the Skin's Caress Fibres
question: What can touch research explain about the feelings a surface evokes, and where does the evidence stop?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column uses the 2025 On Touch workshop by Jonathan Radetz and Babette Wiezorek as a starting point for explaining sensory experience. For readers interested in neuroscience and design, it compares experimenter-applied brush strokes, fingertip exploration of materials and touch following social exclusion. The manuscript describes the methods, sample sizes and measured outcomes, then asks how far those findings can inform a workshop about tactile objects. RN’s role is documentary research, synthesis and explanatory writing; the workshop belongs to its credited designers, and the account is drawn from listings rather than an established visit.

title: Why Does Moving Lift Your Mood?
question: How does research distinguish evidence that exercise changes depressive symptoms from explanations of why it might do so?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column explains how researchers study exercise and mood for readers of the Brain and Body series. It compares two reviews of clinical trials, then examines proposed biological explanations involving BDNF, a protein involved in nerve-cell growth and survival, and the hippocampus, a brain region involved in memory. The draft explains differences between control groups, sample sizes, risk of bias and measured outcomes. It separates blood measurements, human brain scans and experiments in mice so that a possible mechanism is not presented as a demonstrated explanation of mood changes in people. RN’s evidenced role is research synthesis and explanatory writing, not conducting the experiments or delivering treatment.

title: Who Gets a Protected Nervous System?
question: Who receives time, discretion, understandable help and room to recover when institutions place demands on them?
expression: RN’s published Polymath essay develops “protected nervous system” as a Nervous System Aware Governance concept for readers examining work, travel, public services and institutional design. It begins with contrasting airport waiting conditions, then compares paid buffers with ordinary access to assistance, control over work pace, predictable schedules, privacy, complaint resolution and the ability to become unavailable. RN combines labor statistics, research on work and health, surveillance reports and examples from several legal systems to ask how institutions distribute demands and support. The essay distinguishes protective friction, such as a second review, from burdens that organizations create and then charge people to escape. title: The Qualities of Native Medicines
question: Whose knowledge, clinical work and decisions disappear when the history of a medicine is reduced to one discoverer?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay follows the preparation, clinical cases and changing printings of W. B. O’Shaughnessy’s nineteenth-century Indian hemp paper. For readers interested in medical history, attribution and institutional ethics, it begins with Ramjan Khan’s tetanus case and examines whose permission the hospital recorded. It then traces Sanskrit and Persian scholarship, translation, preparation knowledge and clinical observations supplied by named collaborators, before comparing how extracts, revisions and later citations altered their visibility. RN’s contribution is documentary research, comparison of editions, historical interpretation and explanatory writing. The article distinguishes the 1839 Calcutta printing from later journal and London versions, and treats the proposed identification of one pandit as an inference rather than an established identity.

A narrower companion manuscript revisits the case, concurrent treatments and consent record. It remains drafted with no public reading URL, and RN has not decided whether it should be a separate publication or support a video. That companion is attached to this work rather than counted as another original.

title: The Ropes in the Pyramid of Unas
question: How does an uncertain identification of an ancient plant become a confident modern claim?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay investigates the Egyptian plant-word šmšm.t and its later identification as cannabis. For readers interested in the history of medicine, language and evidence, it follows the word through a funerary rope passage, medical prescriptions and an offering liturgy, then compares scholarly interpretations and later retellings. RN’s work combines a reported corpus search, translation from glossed Egyptian and German, comparison of printed editions, historical synthesis and explanatory writing. The essay also examines claims about Tutankhamun’s coffin wreaths and chemical findings in mummies, distinguishing a documented report from a broader claim about the whole tomb or ancient Egypt. A chronology and twenty-four-row claim ledger make the argument and its stated limits visible.

title: Free Access to the Tree of Life
question: What can founding texts, colonial statutes and later testimony establish about Rastafari and the herb—and what remains outside that record?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay follows the relationship between Rastafari, ganja and Jamaican law through two founding texts, the history of Leonard Howell and Pinnacle, statutory amendments and later accounts of religious practice. For readers interested in religion, colonial governance and the history of psychoactive plants, RN compares transmitted texts and printed statutes, reconstructs the chronology through scholarly accounts and separates documents from recollection and inference. The essay distinguishes absence from a text from absence of a belief, and the formalisation of a practice from its origin. A separately published exhibit supplies a 1942 statute page and figure credits; it supports this investigation rather than constituting another work. A narrower unpublished companion compares scriptural, legal and scientific kinds of evidence and examines selected sections of the 1960 university report.

title: Nor Cause the Indians to Take Them
question: What does a prohibition reveal when the court could prosecute people requesting a practice but lacked jurisdiction over many of those performing it?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay examines the Mexican Inquisition’s 1620 peyote edict, its wording and the colonial records used to explain whom it could reach. For readers interested in legal history, Indigenous knowledge and the history of psychoactive plants, RN compares Spanish and Nahuatl passages in the Florentine Codex, Latin descriptions attributed to Hernández, different copies and translations of the edict, archival catalogue descriptions and later scholarship. The essay follows three self-denunciations from San Luis Potosí, distinguishes people who took peyote themselves from those who asked others to take it, and develops an interpretation of the prohibition as a law about delegation. A chronology separates practices, surviving records, publication dates and legal events. RN’s contribution is documentary research, textual comparison, translation and explanatory writing. A narrower unpublished companion examines the edict’s account of visions, its jurisdictional clause and disputed date; it remains supporting material for this work.

title: The Soma That No One Drinks
question: What can a ritual text establish about a lost ingredient when it describes the preparation more fully than the plant?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay follows attempts to identify soma through Vedic hymns, ritual manuals, historical translations, accounts of later practice and archaeological debate. For readers interested in the history of research, religion and psychoactive plants, RN reports a verse-level vocabulary count, compares descriptions of handling with the limited botanical language, and reads instructions for substituting other materials when soma is unavailable. The essay then traces competing identifications, the evidence and translation choices behind them, and an archaeological analysis that did not resolve the original claims. A chronology and a twenty-five-item claim ledger separate the dates of practices, texts and modern interpretations. RN’s evidenced role is textual research, comparison, analysis and explanatory writing. A narrower draft companion introduces the same distinction between what the hymns describe and what their silence can establish; it supports this essay rather than adding another identified plant or completed work.

title: I Tear Up at Every Bluey Episode

expression: RN’s short Formation Notes essay reflects on why quiet episodes of Bluey move her as a parent. title: A Meal on Mushrooms
question: What happens when drug scheduling, food-and-drug classification and food-service regulation meet at a dinner table?
expression: RN’s High Culture essay examines infused dining as a problem shared by several institutions. A narrower prepared companion concentrates on food-effect studies and the limits of the available trial record.

title: What If Air Could Do the Job of a Mold? What the Flax
question: What can exhibition listings and engineering research establish about shaping plant fibres without a conventional mold?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist column examines Benedikt Trojer’s What the Flax project through the Dutch Design Week archive and the designer’s institutional profile. For readers interested in materials, agriculture and design, it connects the described sewn and inflated flax composites with a history of fibre flax and a separate engineering study of robot-wound flax and timber.
