question: How did a hormone involved in birth and nursing come to stand for love and trust? Which experiments actually tested those claims?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist draft for readers who have heard oxytocin called the love hormone. She distinguishes a study of the human receptor’s structure from experiments that measured partner preference in prairie voles. She compares drug-blocking studies with a genetic experiment and a published challenge to what the mutations removed. For the human evidence she follows an early trust-game result into a registered replication: the main test did not find the expected increase in trust.
boundary: The manuscript is a held Fat Nugs Magazine draft, paired with its receptor card. Bonding in the tested voles does not establish that oxytocin has no role in attachment, and a laboratory trust game is not a measure of love. No public manuscript, treatment recommendation or independent scientific clearance is offered.
provenance: The complete draft and its references were compared with the AaN register and paired card record. The registered human replication was checked for its main result. The draft reports the disagreement about the vole experiment without resolving it.

title: The Pool Noodle Test
question: How do you notice a change in yourself when the clearest sign is a reaction you expected but did not have?
expression: In this Formation Notes essay, RN recounts a brief sting that amused her instead of making her angry. She describes the sensation, the reaction she expected and what she noticed in its absence. For readers trying to recognize growth in ordinary moments, she offers a way of paying attention: staying calm need not mean that nothing hurt, and it need not mean hiding an emotion that was there all along.
boundary: The Polymath published the personal essay. RN presents one observation about her own response, not a parenting intervention or evidence of a particular brain mechanism. A later AaN manuscript considers laboratory research on pain and emotion. It remains an unpublished companion and has no reading link here.
provenance: The public article and current publisher record were compared with the separately registered AaN draft. The research belongs to that companion; the original essay does not cite those studies.

title: Why Do You Get Goosebumps? The Alpha-1 Adrenergic Receptor
question: When cold makes a hair stand up, what actually moves? Is that brief movement the same thing as growing a new hair?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist draft for readers curious about a familiar skin reflex. She traces the contraction of the tiny muscle beside a hair follicle, then follows a different signal that sympathetic nerves send to hair-follicle stem cells in mice. The distinction matters: the draft discusses alpha-1 receptors on the muscle and a beta-2 receptor in the mouse stem-cell experiment. RN compares those findings with recordings of human goosebumps and a small anatomical study of human skin.
boundary: The Fat Nugs Magazine manuscript and its accompanying receptor card are held. Recording a goosebump in a person does not establish the hair-growth mechanism found in mice. The draft does not identify a particular alpha-1 subtype on the human muscle or offer hair-loss treatment advice.
provenance: The complete AaN manuscript and its draft register were compared with the paired receptor-card record and the primary mouse study. The card and manuscript describe one editorial package.

title: Why Does Sugar Taste Sweet? TAS1R2 and TAS1R3
question: How can two proteins work together to detect sweetness, and what can a receptor image tell us about what an animal or person actually tastes?
expression: RN compares three kinds of evidence in this Ask a Neuroscientist draft: images of a two-part receptor bound to sweeteners, a disrupted receptor gene in cats, and a human study in which participants ranked sucrose solutions. She explains how researchers locate a binding pocket, why a genetic finding is different from a taste test, and why the human variants studied account for only part of the variation between people.
boundary: The Fat Nugs Magazine manuscript and receptor card remain held. The structures discussed show artificial sweeteners rather than table sugar bound to the receptor. They do not establish how sweet a person would find a substance, and the manuscript makes no dietary recommendation.
provenance: The revised AaN manuscript, owner register and related card were compared. The receptor study was checked for the molecules and constructs actually imaged. Some earlier experiments are reported through later literature in RN’s draft.

title: From Arrow Poison to Surgery
question: What does a plant poison used in hunting have to do with muscle relaxation in an operating room?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist draft around the point where a nerve signals a muscle. She compares a historical review of curare with laboratory research on the receptors its alkaloids block. That comparison lets readers follow the change in setting, from Indigenous South American hunting knowledge to a 1942 surgical report, without confusing paralysis with unconsciousness or pain relief.
boundary: This is an unpublished Fat Nugs draft. The historical review is not a firsthand account from the communities whose knowledge it describes. The gallery offers no preparation, exposure or treatment guidance.
provenance: The full manuscript, its two cited papers and the owner register were identified. The 1942 publication record was checked; sole-credit and route-of-exposure claims in the draft were not carried into this description.

title: Why Fentanyl Can Outlast Naloxone
question: Why can breathing improve after an opioid overdose and then become dangerously slow again?
expression: RN compares two reviews for readers trying to understand what overdose reversal means. She explains how naloxone temporarily competes with opioids at receptors, then uses the reviews’ different estimates of how quickly naloxone leaves the body to distinguish an initial response from lasting recovery. The manuscript discusses why the timing matters without turning an average into a prediction for an individual.
boundary: This is a held Fat Nugs manuscript, not a dosing guide or a clinical trial. It gives no individual prognosis. No public edition or associated media has been verified.
provenance: The full draft and its bibliography were compared with the AaN owner register. The two underlying sources are reviews. No new clinical review or treatment recommendation is claimed.

title: “1 in 12 Boys” Needs a Population
question: Who was counted, and how? What gets lost when a prevalence estimate becomes a slogan?
expression: RN takes a familiar figure about red–green color vision and follows it back to the population it describes. She sets a genetics reference alongside adult screening results from South Korea and preschool testing in Southern California. A reader can see how age, sampling and the difference between a screening result and a confirmed finding change what a percentage means.
boundary: This is an unpublished Polymath essay draft. It is distinct from the Color Vision Field Guide application. It does not use a child’s case or estimate any individual’s likelihood of a diagnosis. The manuscript records that several underlying papers were read as abstracts.
provenance: The full AaN manuscript and its references were compared with the owner register and the existing field-guide description. Population estimates are attributed to their own studies rather than pooled into a universal rate.

title: The Superpower That Depends on the Test
question: When does color distract someone from a camouflaged target, and when does it help them find it?
expression: RN compares three jobs that are often treated as the same test of vision: spotting a geometric target behind red and green visual noise, finding birds or eggs in field photographs, and locating colored fruit at a distance. She distinguishes studies of people with color-vision differences from an online game that changed the images shown to players. The results depend on what the viewer is asked to find, not just on how many color channels the image contains.
boundary: This is a held Polymath manuscript, distinct from the Color Vision Field Guide application. A simulation does not reproduce a lifetime of seeing with a color-vision difference. The studies do not establish a general camouflage advantage for an individual. Two early laboratory papers were not read in full by the source author; their results are described through the later 2017 paper, rather than presented as independently reviewed original studies. Scientific claims, quotations and reuse rights remain unverified here.
provenance: The complete current 7,971-character draft and references, drafted owner row and related guide description were compared November 19, 2026. The manuscript’s November 11 clarification supersedes the earlier abstract-only access wording. RN notes a disagreement between the results and discussion of the photograph study and states which passage she followed. The owner planning date is not a release; no public URL is recorded.

title: Trauma-Informed Architecture
question: How might a corridor, shelter or waiting area feel to someone already on guard, and what choices can a designer give that person?
expression: RN wrote this architecture article for designers working in settings such as supportive housing, youth shelters and refugee camps. She compares layouts that make exits and sightlines easy to read with spaces that impose glare, noise or crowding. Across those examples she asks who can control light, temperature and privacy. She connects those practical decisions to research on stress while keeping residents’ experiences central to the design question.
boundary: This is a published journal article, not a building RN designed or a trial she conducted. The settings and study designs differ: a short virtual-reality experiment cannot establish whether a building improves long-term trauma outcomes. The later social package remains a draft and is not linked here.
provenance: Journal of Biophilic Design, issue 17 (Architecture). RN is the credited author. The article text on Selected Works matches the text used in the later companion package. Its carousel specification and reel script do not establish that either was produced or published.

title: Designing for Cognitive Clarity
question: When a room demands attention from someone already exhausted, which parts of its design could make it easier to concentrate or withdraw?
expression: RN wrote this interiors article for people choosing lighting, materials and layouts in shared spaces. She explains attention restoration through a comparison of visually busy interiors and quieter places with daylight, natural textures and clear routes. She draws on housing and healthcare research, then uses a Boston library renovation to make the choices concrete: a reading nook, an acoustic buffer and a place to sit away from activity.
boundary: This is a published journal article. RN interprets research and built examples; she did not design the library or measure recovery there. Short-term stress measures, residents’ accounts and clinical outcomes are different kinds of evidence. The later social package remains a draft and is not linked here.
provenance: Journal of Biophilic Design, issue 18 (Interior Design). RN is the credited author. The article text on Selected Works matches the text used in the later companion package. Its carousel specification and reel script do not establish that either was produced or published.

title: Biophilic Landscapes as Cognitive Infrastructure
question: Who can actually reach and use a green space, and what makes it usable once they get there?
expression: RN examines landscapes as settings for attention and orientation. She follows a visitor’s practical needs: finding a legible route, recognizing a landmark, resting in shade and reaching a place that feels safe. She compares parks, healthcare landscapes and neighborhood greening studies, asking how maintenance, access and displacement can change who benefits from a design.
boundary: This is a published journal article, not a landscape RN built. Neighborhood associations and trials of particular interventions cannot identify one park feature or amount of exposure that works for every community. The later social package remains a draft and is not linked here.
provenance: Journal of Biophilic Design, issue 20 (Landscape Architecture). RN is the credited author. The article text on Selected Works matches the text used in the later companion package. Its carousel specification and reel script do not establish that either was produced or published.

title: Biophilic Design and Climate Change
question: When extreme heat makes a neighborhood harder to live in, where can people find relief, and who is left out?
expression: RN connects research on heat and mental health with decisions about shade, water, vegetation and access to cooler public places. She explains why an isolated park is different from a network people can reach along everyday routes. She also examines the risk that improvements raise costs for the residents they were meant to serve, and asks how cities might measure cooling and recovery separately.
boundary: This is a published journal article. Its policy and design proposals are not completed interventions. A measured drop in temperature does not by itself establish a mental-health outcome; several case-study figures in the companion still need source checks. The later social package remains a draft and is not linked here.
provenance: Journal of Biophilic Design, issue 21 (Climate Change). RN is the credited author. The article text on Selected Works matches the text used in the later companion package. Its carousel specification and reel script do not establish that either was produced or published.

title: Wood – the Multisensory, Physiological Magician
question: What evidence would justify choosing wood for a room on sensory or climate grounds, rather than simply because people like its appearance?
expression: RN compares the visual, tactile, acoustic and olfactory qualities of wood with findings from studies of stress and attention. She moves from classrooms, healthcare settings and civic interiors to questions that material specifications have to answer: where the timber came from, how it will be maintained and what happens to it at the end of its use. She separates the sensory argument from the carbon-storage argument.
boundary: This is a published journal article, not a material test RN conducted. The studies reviewed do not establish a universal physiological benefit from wood. Carbon claims depend on sourcing and use, and some numerical claims in the derivative package still need verification. The later social package remains a draft and is not linked here.
provenance: Journal of Biophilic Design, issue 22 (Wood). RN is the credited author. The article text on Selected Works matches the text used in the later companion package. Its carousel specification and reel script do not establish that either was produced or published.

title: Why Does a Mosquito Bite Itch?
question: Why can a tiny bite demand so much attention, and what do researchers actually measure when they say scratching brings relief?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist essay for readers curious about an everyday skin reaction. She follows the proposed routes from mosquito saliva to an itch signal, then compares three kinds of evidence: mice scratching after an experimental stimulus, recordings from spinal neurons in monkeys, and people describing their own bites. The comparison shows why a change in a neuron’s activity and a person’s report of relief answer different questions.
boundary: Drafted for the Fat Nugs Magazine column. The monkey experiment used histamine, not mosquito bites; it cannot establish how much relief scratching gives a person. The draft and its receptor card remain held.
provenance: The full AaN manuscript identifies its intended column. The companion card record covers the same question; the two are counted together.

title: Why Does Stress Make Your Heart Pound?
question: Your heart can start pounding as soon as you stand to speak. Is that the same response researchers measure when they take a cortisol sample later?
expression: For this Ask a Neuroscientist essay, RN traces the question from Walter Cannon’s animal experiments to mock interviews and mental arithmetic in human stress studies. She explains what Cannon measured using a strip of intestinal muscle, why that was not a recording of a heartbeat, and how researchers use different measurements for the fast nerve response and the slower hormone response. She then asks what a study following workers over years can say about job strain.
boundary: Drafted for Fat Nugs Magazine. The job-strain study reports an association across groups; it cannot establish what caused an individual’s heart disease. The manuscript flags a remaining full-paper check in its immunity section. The draft and its Brain and Body card remain held.
provenance: The full AaN manuscript identifies its intended column. The companion card record covers the same question; the two are counted together.

title: Why Does Chili Feel Hot?
question: What makes a pepper feel hot even when the food is cool? And why would the same pepper produce a different response in another animal?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist essay about TRPV1, a channel that can respond to both capsaicin and heat. She walks readers through the experiment that made previously unresponsive cells respond to capsaicin, then compares structural studies with observations in chickens, mice and tree shrews. The tree-shrew example lets her separate sensitivity to the chemical in chili from sensitivity to heat itself.
boundary: Drafted for Fat Nugs Magazine. The essay distinguishes animal and cell experiments from human preferences, and treats the suggested evolutionary explanation as a hypothesis. The manuscript and its receptor card remain held; their planning dates differ and do not establish a release.
provenance: The full AaN manuscript identifies its intended column. The companion card record covers the same question; the two are counted together.

title: Could the Next Motorway Be Grown on a Farm? Farming Future Foundations and Nieuw Zwanenburg
question: Could a road, bridge or sound barrier be made from crops grown beside the motorway? What would count as evidence that it works?
expression: RN wrote this Polymath field essay after seeing crates of produce and dried stalks in Building TX at Dutch Design Week. She follows the programme listing to Farming Future Foundations, a Willem de Kooning Academy student exhibition with Nieuw Zwanenburg and Het Nieuwe Instituut. The earlier Harvest of Dreams show explains how the students came to work with farm-grown fibres. RN compares the farm’s flax bridge, sound barrier and trials of plant-based road binder with research on how residents report night-time traffic noise.
boundary: This is a held manuscript. RN’s account says her photograph did not include a title panel, so the listing identifies a plausible show rather than proving what was in the frame. The sleep research did not test the barrier; RN did not design or measure any of the infrastructure.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN long-form register identify one draft without a public reading link. The exhibition programme credits the designers; RN’s work is the reporting and research essay.

title: Can a Heavier Spoon Steady a Shaky Hand?
question: Would a heavier spoon reduce someone’s tremor, spill less food, or simply feel better to use? Those are three different tests.
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist draft for Fat Nugs readers after researching HAK Studio’s JOYN inclusive tableware. Working from the exhibition listing, she compares a Parkinson’s study that measured shaking with an essential-tremor study that measured spills and asked which spoon people preferred. She explains how the shape of a spoon could make a meal easier without changing the underlying tremor.
boundary: RN did not visit the exhibit or test JOYN. The cited studies used other utensils and different groups of participants; they do not establish a benefit for HAK Studio’s product. The manuscript remains held, and its planning date differs from the owner register.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN long-form register identify one draft without a public reading link. The exhibition programme credits the designers; RN’s work is the reporting and research essay.

title: Can Care Technology Feel Warm? Designing With People With Dementia
question: What would it mean for a device to help someone with dementia find their way home or connect with another person while leaving them in control?
expression: RN examines the designs shown by Anna Ouderenzorg and TU/e’s Expertise Center Dementia and Technology. She uses a home-pointing compass and an object that plays familiar sounds to ask who chooses the assistance and when silence might be more welcome. For this Fat Nugs column draft, she compares the designers’ descriptions with family caregivers’ accounts and workshops in which care staff discussed using sounds with residents.
boundary: RN reported on the prototypes; she did not build them or evaluate residents. The workshops gathered staff perspectives about another device. They do not establish that the exhibited sound object improved memory or mood, or that the compass tracked anyone’s location. The manuscript remains held.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN long-form register identify one draft without a public reading link. The exhibition programme credits the designers; RN’s work is the reporting and research essay.

title: Why Does a Smell Bring Back a Memory With So Much Feeling?
question: Why can a smell bring one childhood moment back vividly, even if it prompts fewer memories than a word or picture?
expression: RN uses Cemre Kara’s Archive of Smells, a game in which visitors explored three imagined districts through scent, as the starting point for a Fat Nugs column draft. She compares research on the age, intensity and frequency of memories brought back by different cues. The distinction matters for the reader: a memory can feel powerful once recalled without being easier to retrieve.
boundary: The installation is Kara’s team’s work. RN’s account of it comes from the listing, and the imaging studies she discusses did not test visitors to the installation. The essay is held; it does not claim that a scented environment improves memory or prevents cognitive decline.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN long-form register identify one draft without a public reading link. The exhibition programme credits the designers; RN’s work is the reporting and research essay.

title: Why Does Fast Food Feel So Easy to Choose?
question: How much of a meal choice happens before someone reaches the counter? Could speed, price and familiar cues make a different menu just as appealing?
expression: RN wrote this Ask a Neuroscientist essay about Eat It!, Co/Lab: Hungry for Change’s imagined fast-food counter at Dutch Design Week. She compares two ways of asking why people eat what they do: studies of how seeing food relates to craving and eating, and an inpatient experiment in which adults could eat as much as they wanted from two different menus. She uses that distinction to ask what a shop would actually have to measure to learn whether its design changed customers’ choices.
boundary: This held Fat Nugs draft describes the exhibition from its listing and host materials. The feeding study supplied the meals; participants were not shopping under time or budget constraints. Neither study tested the installation or its proposed alternative menu.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: Why Do Car Rides Make You Sick? Your Inner Ear's Motion Sensors
question: Why can reading a still screen in the back seat feel different from looking out the window when the car is making exactly the same turns?
expression: RN follows that familiar experience from the inner ear to the competing signals the brain receives. She explains how the semicircular canals register turning and how the other balance organs respond to gravity and acceleration. She then compares small laboratory studies of people with reduced balance function, asking what their responses during rotation can tell us about the part the inner ear plays in nausea.
boundary: This Fat Nugs manuscript and its receptor card are held together. The experiments were small, and reduced susceptibility did not mean that nobody felt sick. The draft distinguishes an explanation of sensory conflict from a more speculative evolutionary explanation for vomiting.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: What Changes Under a Field When You Plant Trees in It?
question: If trees or hedges are planted in a farm field, how could someone tell whether the soil stored more carbon, held more water or supported different wildlife?
expression: RN wrote this Polymath essay after researching Biobased Creations’ Possible Landscapes model of the Achterhoek. She compares findings about hedgerows, rows of trees in cropland and trees in pasture. Rather than treating them as one intervention, she asks where researchers sampled soil, what they compared it with and whether a gain in soil carbon implies a useful gain in water storage.
boundary: RN researched the model from its listing and did not visit it. The studies did not test the displayed plans or measure the soil beneath them. The model belongs to its makers; the held manuscript is RN’s contribution.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: From Field to Cord: What a Flax Plot in Eindhoven Shows About One of Our Oldest Crafts
question: Why would students who grew their own flax make cord instead of yarn, and what evidence survives of how people made cord long before modern spinning machinery?
expression: RN traces the Back to the Flax collective’s route from an Eindhoven plot to its sixth exhibition, on cordage and knotting. She explains why limited access to spinning equipment helped shape the brief, follows the steps needed to separate usable fibre from a stalk, and compares the collective’s process with archaeological evidence of twisted fibres. She also asks what research on craft therapy can tell readers about the experience of the handwork itself.
boundary: This is RN’s held Fat Nugs essay about the collective’s work. Archaeological cord is not proof that the ancient makers used flax, and studies of therapy do not isolate the effects of rope-making. The older edition label and differing planning dates do not establish a second essay or a publication.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: Too Dry and Too Wet: Can a City Work Like a Sponge, and Does Heat Change How We Think?
question: Could a neighbourhood that holds rainwater also protect people from the effects of hot nights? What would researchers have to measure to connect those claims?
expression: RN uses Biobased Creations’ Spons/LAB and its city-as-sponge model to connect a Dutch water-policy question with a Boston heat-wave study. She follows the chain from water storage and urban cooling to indoor temperatures and morning cognitive tests, identifying which steps the separate sources actually measured. The result is a science essay for Polymath readers interested in the links between buildings, heat and daily life.
boundary: This held manuscript is the science companion, distinct from the proposed contracts angle. The heat study did not test the model, a Dutch city or a water-retention intervention. The essay offers a research question, not a demonstrated cognitive benefit of sponge-city design.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: Can a Number From 0 to 10 Hold Your Pain?
question: What can a pain drawing tell a clinician that a single number cannot, and how would we know whether better communication changed someone’s care?
expression: RN examines Li Qiu’s (Un)stilled Pain, which invites people to draw pain with transparent symbols at a light table. Working from the academy’s account, RN compares the purpose of that design with research on clinical pain drawings and unequal experiences of pain care. She distinguishes giving a patient more ways to describe pain from showing that a particular tool improves diagnosis or treatment.
boundary: RN did not visit the project or test its symbols. The cited studies concern other tools and settings; none establishes a clinical outcome for Li Qiu’s design. This Fat Nugs manuscript remains held, with no public reading link.
provenance: The current AaN manuscript and its owner register identify this essay as a draft. The related package is counted with the essay; no manuscript or media has been released here.

title: Disgust, Microbes and the Future of Shopping
question: Would a purple fabric look different to a shopper after they learned that yeast made its dye?
expression: RN’s Polymath draft starts with her account of two press tours through the Biodesign Warehouse, the department store curated by Emma van der Leest at Dutch Design Week. RN follows particular objects, including yeast-coloured textiles and an archive of scents made with microbes, into research about disgust, preferences for things described as natural, and how people judge materials by sight. She asks what a retailer would need to observe to know whether explaining how a material was made changed someone’s willingness to buy it.
boundary: The current draft replaces an earlier article about a fungus-grown wall panel. RN reported on the exhibition; she did not design the products or measure shoppers’ reactions. A separate public-health pop-up studied attitudes toward hygiene, not demand for microbial goods. The essay, photographs and recordings remain unlinked.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: Can Clay Walls Change How a Room Feels?
question: A piece of clay plaster can absorb moisture in a lab. Would someone living with a clay wall actually notice a difference in the air?
expression: RN uses the Dutch exhibition on fifty years of biological and biobased building to frame a question for readers interested in materials and indoor comfort. She compares three distinct tests: how a sample handles moisture, how people rate air at different temperatures and humidity levels, and how air was rated in a chamber with clay plaster. She proposes a way to close the gap: compare occupied rooms across seasons, measuring humidity alongside residents’ own ratings.
boundary: This held Fat Nugs draft describes the exhibition from its programme; RN did not visit it. The studies did not test the exhibited buildings or establish that a clay wall prevents damp or improves residents’ health.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: Why Does One Sweater Feel Soft and Another Itch?
question: If a knitted material looks soft on a shelf, what could tell a designer how it will feel against skin?
expression: RN starts with Welded Loop Biobased, in which Studio Joris de Groot and Knit in Motion explored knitting and welding a plant-based plastic for accessories. She compares tests of wool knit structure and fibre thickness with studies that recorded brain responses while people rated fabrics. She also looks at what a small clothing trial in children can and cannot tell a designer choosing a material.
boundary: RN researched the exhibition from its listing. The studies involved other fabrics; they did not test a Welded Loop shoe or establish how its plastic feels. The manuscript is held and does not recommend a treatment or garment.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: Why Can Red and Green Look Alike? The Cone Opsins Behind Colour Vision
question: What can the genes for colour vision tell us about why two lights look alike to one person and different to another?
expression: RN follows three light-sensitive proteins in the retina from early colour-matching observations to studies of the genes that encode them. She compares genetic findings about the red- and green-sensitive pigments with John Dalton’s account of his own vision and a later review of DNA recovered from his preserved eye. The essay asks what each kind of evidence can answer: a gene or protein structure is different from a person’s report of what a colour looks like.
boundary: The held Fat Nugs manuscript and receptor card form one teaching package. RN’s revised account of Dalton draws on a later review, and the tissue came from one person. This is a separate essay from RN’s prevalence and camouflage essays or the Color Vision Field Guide.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: Why Does Time Seem to Slow Down or Speed Up?
question: When a frightening moment seems to last forever, is more detail available at the time, or does the moment seem longer in memory?
expression: RN uses Kanghui Zhang’s three-screen installation Threading, Drifting, and Sensing to separate three questions that sound alike. She follows what people remembered after a frightening fall, how long a moving pattern appeared to last in a lab, and how quickly people said time was passing during everyday activities. Those studies measured different experiences, so RN explains why they cannot all be treated as readings of the same clock.
boundary: This Fat Nugs draft draws on the exhibition listing. None of the studies tested Zhang’s screens, and an association between mood and time passing does not establish cause. The manuscript and owner register give different planning dates; neither is a release.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: Does the Colour of Your Bedding Matter to a Sleeping Brain?
question: Does the colour printed on a duvet affect sleep in the same way as light reaching someone’s eyes before bed?
expression: RN takes Studio RENS and Auping’s CANVAS bedding as the starting point for a Fat Nugs essay about what sleep experiments actually measure. She distinguishes printed pigment from a light source, compares studies of evening light and screens with research on bedding materials and temperature, and asks what evidence would be needed to isolate an effect of hue. A coloured surface can only reflect light that reaches it.
boundary: RN did not see the collection; her design account comes from the programme. The studies she located do not compare sleep under different duvet colours. Her draft and the owner register list different planning dates. Neither the manuscript nor collection media is linked.
provenance: The current manuscript and AaN’s owner register identify this as a draft with no public reading URL. Related package material is counted with the essay.

title: What a Drug Schedule Weighs: The Science Behind Moving Cannabis to Schedule III
question: What does a drug schedule tell readers about evidence of harm, dependence and medical use, and what does it leave unresolved?
expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist manuscript, intended for The Polymath, explains the scientific questions behind the 2023 federal cannabis review. She compares measures of adverse outcomes, explains why adjusting for how often a substance is used changes a comparison, and separates accepted medical use for scheduling from the evidence required to approve a drug product. The draft puts the review’s comparative findings alongside its descriptive-data limitations, its exception for young children and a dated account of dependence and withdrawal. RN’s work is research synthesis and public explanation. It is a science companion to her separate Federal Drug Policy, April 2026 brief, whose focus is the legal architecture; the two texts answer different questions.
boundary: The manuscript remains a draft, with no recorded publication URL. Its November 11 revision attributes the HHS findings through the 2024 proposed rule because the underlying HHS PDF was unavailable to its author. The legal timeline stops at the reported September 2026 stay and is not a current compliance guide. Targeted checks corroborated the proposed rule’s methodological cautions and the April 2026 order’s limited scope and effective date; they did not verify every scientific claim, later procedural development or quoted statistic. The 2018 dependence estimates need their dates preserved. RN has not decided whether this manuscript will be published separately or used only for video. No manuscript or media is released here.
provenance: Complete current manuscript and AaN owner record reviewed November 11, 2026, with targeted Federal Register passages. The separately published legal brief was located but not fully reviewed or added as a second gallery entry in this batch. Scheduled adaptations count with this manuscript; source and derivative release decisions remain with their owners.

title: Seeing Ghosts and Running About
question: How did a sentence transmitted through competing editions become a claim that an emperor recorded cannabis intoxication thousands of years earlier?
expression: RN’s Herbal Histories essay follows a famous hemp passage through Chinese medical texts and their later reconstructions. For readers encountering the familiar Shennong story, she compares the editions associated with Sun Xingyan and Mori Risshi, translates disputed wording and follows the role of red ink and reversed type in separating layers of a text. title: Does Growth Mindset Work?
question: What do growth-mindset studies measure, and which students and settings do their findings describe?
expression: RN’s draft distinguishes the association between beliefs and achievement from the effect of an intervention intended to change those beliefs. It compares two pooled analyses with a brief online intervention in United States secondary schools, explaining the differences among studies, samples and individual effect estimates. For readers assessing education claims, RN focuses on average results, lower-achieving students, school context and the limits of extending one short lesson into a universal programme.
boundary: Unpublished, release-held Ask a Neuroscientist draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine. The source review is explicitly based on abstracts; full-text effect sizes were not read, and the older headline claim of about one percent is omitted. Subgroup and peer-context findings do not establish a general workplace or year-long programme effect. Strong-subgroup wording, causal interpretations of context and advice to target and measure need further source-owner review. Complete manuscript review is not independent scientific, statistical, disclosure or rights acceptance. No manuscript or publication link is exposed.
provenance: Complete manuscript and references were read in the preceding continuation. Current source revision and drafted owner record reconfirmed November 19, 2026; Fat Nugs routing, blank public URL and planning-date status retained.

title: Left Brain, Right Brain
question: How did evidence that brain regions specialize become a story about two kinds of person?
expression: RN’s draft traces the left-brain/right-brain personality story through historical language research, split-brain studies, a Nobel lecture and later brain-imaging work. For readers evaluating popular neuroscience, RN compares regional specialization with claims about a person’s overall thinking style. The essay also examines handedness, creativity and the limits of applying findings from people with surgically separated hemispheres to the general population.
boundary: Unpublished, release-held Ask a Neuroscientist draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine. The complete manuscript, captions and references have been read for this description; the underlying papers, historical quotations, translations, images and rights have not been independently cleared. The 1,011-person resting-network study discussed here did not measure personality or thinking style, so it is not a direct personality test. Split-brain interpretations remain disputed, and the creativity reviews do not establish a simple hemisphere-based rule. Survey-chart labels and comparisons still need review. No manuscript or publication link is supplied.
provenance: Complete source reviewed in continuation112; current manuscript and drafted owner record reconfirmed November 19, 2026. The earlier creative-hemisphere title identifies the same work. The owner’s future date is a plan, and its public URL is blank.

title: Why Does a Room Go Still?
question: What can measurements of an audience’s heart rhythms and facial expressions tell us about a shared experience?
expression: RN’s draft compares a concert study of live and simultaneous livestream audiences with a theater study of facial-expression synchrony. For readers curious about collective attention, RN explains how researchers measure similarity between people over time, distinguishes heart-monitor participants from the broader questionnaire sample, and separates audience reports from a dramaturge’s predictions of engagement. The essay uses these differences to examine what a shared room might add while leaving its opening question about collective stillness unresolved.
boundary: Unpublished, release-held Ask a Neuroscientist draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine. The complete manuscript and references were read, but the underlying studies have not received a complete independent review in this recovery pass. Neither study directly measures shared stillness. Similar responses do not by themselves establish mutual influence, a common feeling or a cause of a room becoming quiet. A failure to detect a seating effect does not establish that seat location never matters. Stronger causal, seating and participant-comparison statements in the manuscript remain for source-owner review. Image and rights acceptance is not established. No manuscript or publication link is supplied.
provenance: Complete 8,068-character manuscript reviewed in continuation113. Current source revision and drafted owner record reconfirmed November 19, 2026; Fat Nugs routing, blank public URL and planning-date status retained.

title: The Bacterium That Edits Plants
question: How did bacteria that cause plant disease or affect insects become tools for biotechnology?
expression: RN’s draft pairs Agrobacterium’s transfer of DNA into plants with the insect-targeting proteins made by Bacillus thuringiensis. For readers unfamiliar with plant biotechnology, RN explains plasmids, transferred DNA, crown gall, Cry proteins and promoters, then separates the natural processes from their research and agricultural applications. A promoter experiment and an image-source exception show why the identity of the organism and the scope of each study matter.
boundary: Unpublished draft intended for The Polymath, recovered from the Ask a Neuroscientist source collection. The complete manuscript and five references were read for this description; underlying papers, experiments, images and rights have not received full independent review. Historical Bti resistance and safety statements are attributed to a 2014 mosquito-control review and cannot establish current safety or resistance across crops and ecosystems. The manuscript’s broader environmental language, image-panel identity and citation-version details remain for source-owner review. It does not provide pest-control or genetic-engineering instructions. No manuscript or publication link is supplied.
provenance: Complete source reviewed November 19, 2026. The older Bt and crown gall idea title identifies this manuscript. Owner record remains drafted, with a blank public URL and a future planning date.

title: What Biochar Does in Soil
question: What changes when biochar is judged for plant nutrition rather than carbon storage?
expression: RN’s draft compares a crop-nutrient meta-analysis with a perspective on biochar’s different purposes. For readers evaluating claims about soil amendments, RN separates plant biomass, total nutrient accumulation and nutrient concentration, then considers variation between elements, crops and biochar properties. The essay uses that comparison to explain why evidence of soil benefits and evidence of durable carbon storage answer different questions.
boundary: Unpublished Ask a Neuroscientist draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine. The manuscript describes 144 paired observations rather than 144 independent studies; its averages cannot predict a particular field or product. No application rates, production instructions, product recommendation or publication link is supplied.

title: Digging In Together
question: What does gardening research actually tell us about loneliness in older adults?
expression: RN’s draft compares a broad gardening meta-analysis with a review of nature-based programs for older adults. For readers interested in community activities and care settings, it separates mood, life satisfaction, sense of community and loneliness, explains publication-bias checks and evidence certainty, and asks whether company and shared activity could account for some benefits attributed to plants. The shared-activity explanation is presented as a hypothesis, not an established mechanism.

Study-level results, its low-risk characterization, named care programs, images and rights remain unverified. This is an explanatory essay, not a delivered program, treatment recommendation or proven loneliness intervention. No manuscript or publication link is supplied.

title: What the Chatbot Trials Show
question: What can early chatbot trials tell readers about mental-health outcomes, and what remains unknown about safety and lasting benefit?
expression: RN’s draft compares two research reviews from 2020 and 2023 for readers trying to understand claims about mental-health chatbots. It explains the difference between symptom scores and wider well-being, what randomized comparisons add, and why statistical improvement is not automatically a meaningful change in daily life. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing, including a discussion of user experience and the limits of treating a human–AI relationship as an explanation for clinical outcomes.

title: Can a Robot Be a Friend?
question: How do children distinguish talking machines from people while still treating them as sources of knowledge, comfort or friendship?
expression: RN’s draft brings together a laboratory study of a humanoid robot, later accounts of a voice-assistant study and a scoping review of conversational AI. For readers trying to understand claims about children and AI companions, it separates social behavior, selective trust and moral standing: treating a robot fairly is different from granting it every human right. It also distinguishes a short interaction from evidence about development over years. RN’s contribution is explanatory research synthesis, including an account of what a scoping review maps and what these different technologies and study designs cannot establish together.

title: Kids, AI and the Developing Brain
question: What does research on young people's AI use actually measure, and how far is it from evidence about brain development?
expression: RN’s draft compares a study using parental device-monitoring data with a review of adolescent mental-health research. It explains age-group usage, the difference between a median and an average, and why a small group of heavy users can be obscured by a single summary. It then separates associations measured at one time from evidence that follows children over time. For readers interpreting claims about children and AI, RN’s contribution is a research-based explanation of the gap between the question in the title and what the cited studies measured.

title: Time in the Brain: How the Brain Keeps Time, and Why It Bends
question: What can research on timing, emotion and memory tell designers about the pace of an experience, and where does that evidence stop?
expression: RN’s draft brings several kinds of time-perception research into a discussion of experience design. It moves from proposed brain mechanisms and body signals to emotion, remembered fear, laboratory studies of altered states and shared arousal during a ritual. RN compares what each study measured, its participants and its limits, then asks how cautiously those findings can inform the pacing of festivals, rituals or immersive spaces. Her contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing for designers, with a distinction between an interesting design possibility and an effect that has actually been tested.
boundary: Unpublished Ask a Neuroscientist essay intended for Polymath’s Psychedelics Design 2026 coverage. The research log reports reading six papers and a correction, but this portfolio review has not independently verified those papers, quotations or claims. Small samples, animal-to-human comparisons, funding disclosures and the gap between laboratory tasks and designed experiences remain material limits. Shared heart-rate patterns do not establish altered felt time. The manuscript’s statement that no rigorous pacing study was found is limited to its search, not an exhaustive absence claim. No drug-use advice, validated design method, completed media package or cleared imagery is supplied.

title: Can Software Read a Child’s Emotions?
question: What has emotion-recognition software actually been tested against, and what does that tell us about claims to read a child’s feelings?
expression: RN’s draft compares a review of facial expressions, a study of software classifying posed and acted faces, and a study comparing software with trained observers of infants. For readers assessing monitoring claims in classrooms or homes, she explains why the face, setting, age group and comparison method matter. The essay separates matching a human observer’s expression label from knowing someone’s internal emotional state, and distinguishes a test on movie stills from evidence about children’s everyday behaviour. RN’s contribution is research-based explanation and a set of questions about how a claim was tested.
boundary: Unpublished Ask a Neuroscientist essay intended for Fat Nugs Magazine. None of the reviewed studies tested school-age classroom use, and the draft is not an evaluation of current products. The infant study used human expression coding as its comparison; that is not direct access to the infant’s feelings. Sparse negative expressions, age-range mismatch, classification measures and untested demographic biases remain important limits. The research log retains an abstract-based opening and later full-text reports, plus an older claim calling acted movie expressions natural; those records need reconciliation. This portfolio review has not independently verified the papers, numerical findings, quotations, recommendations, media or rights. No manuscript or publication link is supplied.

title: Cesalpino: Sorting Plants by Fruit and Seed
question: How does choosing which features count change the way we group plants?
expression: RN’s draft reads a classification rule in Andrea Cesalpino’s De plantis and follows how that rule organizes later sections of the book. It explains counts of seeds and seed cases, then compares the importance given to position and shape with the treatment of colour, smell, taste and medicinal use. Written for readers interested in botany and how people organize knowledge, RN’s contribution is a close reading and plain-language interpretation of a historical method. The manuscript also describes four later botanical plates and a supporting sorting activity; those supporting elements belong to the same work.

title: The Self and Its Edges
question: What can researchers measure when someone feels that the boundary of their self has changed?
expression: RN’s draft brings together questionnaires about the sense of self, brain-imaging studies, experiments in feeling ownership of an artificial body, and a shared virtual-reality experience. Written for readers interested in immersive art and design, it explains how these different methods approach experiences often called ego dissolution: a weakening of the usual feeling of being a separate self. RN’s contribution is a comparative research synthesis that separates what a method measures from the explanation attached to it. The essay follows the disagreement over suggestion in the rubber-hand illusion and asks how a designer could test the contribution of a particular feature of an experience.
boundary: Unpublished Ask a Neuroscientist essay prepared for Polymath’s Psychedelics Design Conference coverage. title: How Does Your Hand Judge a Material?
question: What can touching a material tell us, and where do laboratory measurements stop short of a design exhibition?
expression: RN’s draft uses the Biomaterials Library: Lithuanian & Baltic Creators as a starting point for explaining material perception. For readers interested in design and the senses, it compares experiments on detecting tiny surface patterns, describing different kinds of softness, seeing a hand manipulate a material, and measuring responses to pleasant or unpleasant touch. A further section separates these sensory questions from research on the physical strength of mycelium-bound composites. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing that connects a documented exhibition to questions the studies can address, while keeping the exhibition’s creators and their work distinct from her analysis.

title: Reishi and Mood: What the Studies Actually Show
question: How should a reader compare claims about reishi and mood when studies use different fungi, preparations and groups of people?
expression: RN’s draft begins with an ethnomycology talk and develops a comparison of a fungal classification paper, one rat study and two small human trials. For readers trying to understand supplement research, it explains why the name of a fungus, the material tested, the participants, the outcome measure and the comparison group all matter. RN’s contribution is a plain-language evidence comparison: distinguishing a change within one group from a difference against placebo, separating mood scores from a diagnosis, and keeping animal findings apart from human treatment claims. The talk supplies context; it does not establish the clinical findings.
boundary: Unpublished Ask a Neuroscientist essay intended for Polymath. The manuscript describes short trials in two specific groups of women, different preparations and conflicting results; it does not establish that reishi treats depression or that products sold under the same common name are interchangeable. It preserves uncertainty over species identification, a proposed mechanism from animal work, and the animal-study authors’ relationship with the extract supplier. The selected studies are not a systematic review of every relevant trial. title: The THC in a Medicine
question: What does the word synthetic tell a reader about a cannabinoid, and what evidence is needed beyond that label?
expression: RN’s draft compares a review of clinical trials involving dronabinol and nabilone with a public-health review of unregulated synthetic cannabinoid products. For general readers of Ask a Neuroscientist, it explains the terminology, introduces receptor activation and separates controlled trial findings from reports of harm outside a trial. RN’s contribution is explanatory research synthesis: showing why findings about a particular medicine, molecule or study population cannot simply be transferred to another product. The essay also explains why pooled adverse-event results and population reports answer different questions.

The research log’s full-reading and confirmed-claim labels are source reports, not independent scientific or legal acceptance by this portfolio review. title: Where Do Your Eyes Go in a Huge Painting?
question: Can an eye-tracking study of pictures on a screen help frame questions about looking at a large fresco?
expression: RN’s draft brings the Triumph of Death in Pisa into conversation with a laboratory study of how people look at paintings. For readers interested in art, perception and travel, it describes the fresco’s disputed attribution and restoration history, then explains the study’s viewing tasks, gaze clusters and fixation measurements. RN’s contribution is a historical and scientific synthesis that turns the comparison into a proposed observation: whether still figures, moving bodies and landscape passages draw attention differently. The essay explicitly presents that application to the fresco as an untested hypothesis.

title: Where does the captured pollution go next?
question: After a device captures tire dust, who receives the collected material and what happens to it?
expression: RN’s Dutch Design Week essay uses VENTRA, a student-built electric concept car, to examine the gap between collecting pollution and accounting for its destination. For readers interested in design and environmental claims, RN compares the makers’ simulation figures, descriptions of the collection system and an enamel demonstration with vehicle rules, waste-law terminology, older Dutch emissions estimates and a different company’s reported experiments. The contribution is a documentary comparison and a set of practical reporting questions: what was collected, how much, under which conditions, what entered a new material and where the remainder went. The essay distinguishes the device, the collected material and its next destination.

title: Who Paid for This Study?
question: What can research funding tell a reader about a health study, and what still needs checking in the study itself?
expression: RN’s draft explains how to read research about industry sponsorship without treating a funding disclosure as a verdict on an individual paper. For readers evaluating health claims, it compares a Cochrane review of sponsorship and study outcomes with an older review discussed through later sources. The essay separates reported results from authors’ conclusions, examines publication and data-access restrictions, and turns those distinctions into questions a reader can ask about sponsors, methods and the fit between evidence and conclusions. RN’s contribution is an explanatory synthesis of existing research, not a new study or an investigation of a particular company.

title: Fire, 1944: Putting a Fresco Back on Its Wall
question: How did the wartime damage to Pisa’s Camposanto lead to decades of rescue, restoration and further repair?
expression: RN’s draft traces the relationship between a damaged building, its wall paintings and the materials used to preserve them. For readers interested in art, history and design, it brings together two university accounts and the Pisa section of a postwar preservation report, moving from the 1944 roof fire through emergency protection, removal of paintings, discovery of preparatory drawings and later restoration campaigns. RN’s contribution is a documentary narrative showing why an early rescue can become part of a later conservation problem. The essay distinguishes the long history of the overall campaign from the treatment history of any one painting.

title: Arches in a Row: Why Repetition Reads as Order
question: Why can repeated architectural details look like one organized whole, and how far can laboratory findings explain that impression?
expression: RN’s draft uses the rows of arches on Pisa’s monuments to introduce research on how viewers group separate shapes. For readers interested in architecture, perception and design, it explains how experiments vary the spacing and similarity of dots, compare competing groupings and test what changes when visual cues agree or conflict. Two research reviews provide the basis for a plain-language account of repetition, symmetry and other forms of regularity. RN’s contribution is to connect those abstract experiments to a question a reader can ask of a building, while marking the architectural application as an interpretation.

title: A Bell Shaped Like a Cone: What Your Brain Hears, and What Your Body Feels
question: What can studies of pitch and felt vibration explain about a room built around resonant objects—and what have they not tested?
expression: RN’s draft introduces Harmen Brethouwer’s Bell Bronzes and the Design by Resonance programme through venue, event and collection records. For readers interested in music, perception and design, it compares laboratory pitch tasks, movement at a concert with very low bass, timing on a vibrating platform and engagement in a vibrating chair. It also examines a venue’s claim about music training and discusses the limits of applying singing-bowl and synchronized-movement research to a performance space. RN’s contribution is documentary research, comparison and explanatory writing; the instruments, exhibition and performances belong to their credited makers.

title: Why a Mushroom Makes Psilocybin: Four Enzymes, Jumping Genes and an Open Question
question: What can fungal chemistry and evolutionary research explain about psilocybin, and what remains unknown about its role in nature?
expression: RN’s draft shifts attention from human experiences to the fungi themselves. For readers of science and design, it brings together studies of fungal genes, museum specimens, bruising chemistry and insect pathogens. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing: organizing the findings, explaining unfamiliar terms and separating laboratory observations from historical estimates and ecological hypotheses. The package includes a long-form manuscript, a research log, a supporting dossier, social adaptations and a six-state educational interactive. These are parts of one work rather than separate publications.

title: Lean On: A Room Built from Everyday Habits, and How Long a Habit Really Takes
question: What does research on forming habits help us notice about the settings of everyday life?
expression: RN’s essay brings Huis Saai’s Lean On exhibition at Dutch Design Week into conversation with a review of health-behaviour habits. For readers interested in design and everyday behaviour, it explains the difference between repeating an action and having it feel automatic, examines the familiar claim that a habit takes 21 days, and compares studies that used different definitions and timelines. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing, connecting the exhibition’s domestic objects and stories to questions about context and repetition. RN did not design the exhibition or conduct the cited experiments. The recovered package contains a long-form manuscript, research notes, a supporting dossier and social adaptations; these belong to one essay.
boundary: Unpublished Polymath draft in the Ask a Neuroscientist programme, planned for March 4, 2027. expression: RN’s Fat Nugs Magazine essay introduces hemp-lime and mycelium composites to readers interested in materials, design and neuroscience. title: The Celebrity Psychedelic Memoir Is a Genre Now
question: How do celebrity accounts of psychedelics become redemption stories, and what do those stories leave out about evidence, access and the people providing the experience?
expression: RN’s High Culture essay examines a recurring pattern in celebrity memoirs, interviews and filmed accounts of psychedelic experiences. Written for readers interested in culture, neuroscience and institutions, its five sections compare the narrative formula with brain research, the retreat economy, Indigenous healers’ accounts and legal records. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and cultural and legal analysis: bringing different kinds of evidence together while distinguishing public testimony, scientific studies, marketing and secondary reporting. title: Why Does Wasabi Sting? The Receptor Called TRPA1

expression: RN’s draft Ask a Neuroscientist essay starts with an everyday sensation and follows the research used to explain it. title: A Richer Cage and an Adult Lazy Eye: Visual Neuroscience from Pisa

title: Does a Psychedelic Trip Scramble Your Brain? The Entropic Brain Debate

expression: RN’s draft for the Ask a Neuroscientist column at Fat Nugs Magazine uses the entropic brain debate to explain how neuroscience claims are made and challenged. title: Why Can a Virtual Room Make Your Stomach Turn? VR and the Body

title: The Midwife Who Was Not There
question: How did a claim about cannabis and medieval childbirth become familiar, and what do the texts cited in its support actually say?
expression: RN’s published Herbal Histories essay investigates a recurring story about medieval European midwives, cannabis and the suppression of women’s medical knowledge. Written for readers of plant history and the history of medicine, it starts with an Anglo-Saxon remedy printed by Thomas Oswald Cockayne, including the editor’s uncertainty about which plant it describes. RN compares named medical texts, traces later accounts of witch trials and women healers, and follows how execution estimates, pamphlets and drug histories contributed to the story. The work combines historical research, writing, author-labelled translations and an evidence-status section that separates direct reading from second-hand accounts and missing sources. A narrower unpublished companion uses the same investigation to explain how to check a health story: read the original passage, preserve uncertainty about the plant, distinguish a recorded recipe from evidence that it worked, and state the limits of a search.
boundary: The original essay is published on Polymath; the related companion remains a draft and is included here as supporting work. This portfolio review establishes the work’s scope and publication, not independent historical, botanical, translation or rights clearance. The companion’s claims and planned media still need editorial review; derivative materials remain held. This is historical writing, not advice on using a remedy.

title: Would a Drink Feel Different in a Glass Grown From Fungus?

expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses Bar Mycelium at Dutch Design Week as a starting point for general readers curious about materials and perception. title: Does the Spring Clock Change Raise the Risk of a Heart Attack?
question: How should a reader interpret headlines linking the spring clock change to heart attacks?
expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist essay compares two research reviews and a Michigan hospital registry study to explain why a striking daily headline can differ from a weekly result. Written for general readers and intended for Polymath, the draft separates spring from autumn transitions, daily counts from weekly totals, and relative changes from an individual person’s risk. It ends with three questions for reading a headline: which seasonal change was studied, how long researchers counted outcomes, and whether they used a fair comparison period. An eight-slide sequence and platform adaptations support the same essay.

title: Why Do Leaf Patterns Catch the Eye? Ecoprints and the Science of Fractals
question: What can research on visual patterns tell us about the appeal of a leaf print on cloth?
expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses LEAF&LOOM’s botanical textiles as a starting point for explaining visual preference to general readers and people interested in design. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing; the textile work belongs to artist Nihan Elmacı Başaran and her studio. The draft introduces fractals as patterns whose parts resemble one another at different scales, then compares two student studies of computer-generated patterns. It explains how an average preference for middle complexity can conceal strong differences between individuals, and why finding a pattern engaging is different from finding it relaxing. A separate discussion considers measurements of branching in artworks. The final section compares the maker’s natural-dye description with a review of textile dyes, distinguishing an attractive print from one that retains its colour. An eight-slide sequence and platform copy adapt the same essay. Later supporting copy proposes additional explanations of mordants, the substances used to help dyes bind to fibres, and the meaning of “chemical-free”; its longer essay and video additions remain outlines.

title: Anatomy in Renaissance Pisa: Realdo Colombo, a Candle and the Blood’s Path Through the Lung
question: How can an anatomist’s own account reveal both the value of observation and the limits of a claim to discovery?
expression: RN’s historical essay follows Pisa’s anatomy school through university and museum histories, selected passages from Realdo Colombo’s 1559 De re anatomica, and a later history of pulmonary circulation—the passage of blood through the lungs. Intended for general readers of Polymath, it connects the school’s teaching history with two stories Colombo tells about testing inherited ideas: melting fat with a candle in Pisa’s theatre and breaking lion bones in Florence to look for marrow. RN’s contribution is documentary comparison, explanatory writing and the package’s attributed translations from selected Latin passages, rather than a new medical finding or an eyewitness account. The essay then examines Colombo’s description of blood passing through the lung alongside his claim that nobody had previously written about it. A secondary history supplies the comparison with Ibn al-Nafis, Servetus, Cesalpino and Harvey. The closing sections examine the anatomy museum’s later collections and preserve conflicting institutional dates instead of choosing an unsupported opening year. A six-slide sequence, archive-image plan and short video script adapt this same work.

title: How a Starling Flock Turns as One: Six or Seven Neighbours Over Rome
question: Does a bird follow every neighbour within reach, or a fixed number of its nearest neighbours?
expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist essay explains a field study of starling flocks over Rome for general readers of Polymath. RN’s contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing, not collecting the bird observations. The draft follows the researchers’ camera setup, their reconstruction of birds’ positions in three dimensions, and their selection of ten flocks from a much larger collection of recordings. It explains the difference between a fixed distance and a fixed number of neighbours, then separates the measured spatial relationships from the researchers’ computer simulation and proposed explanations. A supporting interactive lets a reader spread a drawn group of 140 dots, choose a fixed reach or seven nearest neighbours, and select another focal bird. It illustrates the two rules with generated positions rather than reproducing the study’s data or simulating an actual flying flock. Seven slides, platform copy and a filming plan adapt the same essay; they are not separate works.

title: Who Answers When a Trip Gets Hard? What 25,419 Support Conversations Show

title: How a Plant Seals a Cut

expression: RN’s research and writing package explains plant wound responses for general readers and gardeners. title: Can You Hear an AI Voice Clone?
question: How well can listeners distinguish an AI-cloned voice from a human voice, and what do those judgments tell us about trust?
expression: RN's draft Ask a Neuroscientist column explains how listeners judge AI-cloned voices. It compares two 2025 papers, separating whether a voice sounds like a particular person from whether it sounds human, then examines perceived realism, dominance and trustworthiness. For general readers concerned about trust in calls, RN translates the experimental tasks and their limitations into plain language. A nine-slide sequence, charts, platform copy and video scripts support the same essay. The linked AI Field Notes inventory describes a prepared comparison of human and AI narration; that protocol is distinct from this explanation of other researchers' studies.
boundary: Drafted and held, with no verified publication URL. These online listening studies used short clips and selected cloning systems; their results do not establish performance in every phone call or with later systems. Identity and detection groups must stay distinct, and generic synthetic voices must not be conflated with cloned voices. The suggested second-channel check was not evaluated by the studies. Scientific claims, quoted percentages, figure rights and actual media have not been independently cleared in this intake. Planning dates and production versions disagree; the filming script includes a price claim absent from the reviewed claim log and outdated imagery wording. RN's work is research synthesis and writing, not a voice detector, RN-run listening experiment or completed recording.
provenance: The complete manuscript, research log, dossier and filming notes were reviewed, followed by the platform copy and image metadata. Source-owner full-text and rights-check labels remain attributed evidence. The current AI Field Notes record was compared to distinguish a prepared narration protocol from this essay. Actual source figures, rendered media and recordings were not independently inspected. No draft reading link, source manuscript or private recording is reproduced.

title: What a Dying Cancer Cell Looks Like, and Why It Isn't a Cure
question: What can images of dying cancer cells tell a general reader, and what evidence is still needed before a laboratory result becomes a treatment?
expression: RN's draft Polymath column for Ask a Neuroscientist explains how to read images from a 2019 laboratory study of leukemia cell lines exposed to purified cannabidiol. It walks readers through the study's cell models, untreated comparisons, microscope images and measures of cell damage, then places those findings alongside the much longer process of testing a treatment. RN's contribution is research synthesis and science writing: making the difference between a striking image and evidence of benefit in people understandable. A seven-slide sequence, platform copy and video scripts support the same essay. The proposed interactive explanation of laboratory, animal and human evidence remains an unbuilt idea within this package.
boundary: Drafted and held, with no verified publication URL. The underlying experiment concerns cells in dishes, not treatment of animals or patients; RN did not conduct it. The manuscript distinguishes resting from activated healthy cells, representative experimental images from population estimates, and a computer prediction of protein binding from a demonstrated interaction. It does not establish a treatment, a safe human dose or a reason to use a cannabis product. Scientific claims, figure rights, source-image fidelity and finished media have not been independently cleared in this intake. Planning dates and image counts disagree, and a filming cue points to a slide about a different cell comparison. Those source and production gaps remain unresolved.
provenance: The complete manuscript, research log, dossier, filming notes, image-audit text and production-set text were reviewed. title: What a Festival Day Does to Your Ears
question: What do two festival studies reveal about the difference between hearing a quiet sound and measuring the hearing nerve's response after a loud day?
expression: RN's draft Ask a Neuroscientist column compares two studies of hearing after a music festival. For general readers and event producers, it explains the different measurements: the quietest tones a person can hear and an electrical response associated with the hearing nerve. RN follows each study's participants, exposure and testing schedule, then explains why one test can remain unchanged while another records a difference. Her contribution is research synthesis and plain-language science writing, not conducting the experiments. A nine-slide sequence, charts and diagram instructions, platform copy, video scripts and a proposed scroll-page treatment support the same essay.
boundary: Drafted and held, with no verified publication URL. The studies involved small groups and limited follow-up; their findings do not establish the consequences of repeated festival visits, prove that no lasting injury occurred or show that everyone recovers on the same schedule. A change in the nerve-response measure is not a direct image of lost nerve connections. Behavioral associations must not become causal claims. The manuscript, research log and filming notes differ on study-design details and which statistics were reported; planning dates, reshare timing and visual cues also need reconciliation. Scientific claims, actual figures, rights and finished media have not been independently cleared in this intake. This is an explanatory draft, not an RN-run hearing study, clinical service or completed film.
provenance: The complete manuscript, research log and filming notes were reviewed in the preceding intake.
