title: Foxglove: From a Family Recipe to a Counted Medicine
question: What can a historical account of foxglove teach readers about reporting failures, recording harm and distinguishing a case record from a controlled trial?
expression: RN's draft Polymath essay for Ask a Neuroscientist traces how William Withering described a family remedy and his subsequent work with foxglove. It focuses on his stated decision to report unsuccessful cases alongside successful ones, using passages from his 1785 book, a botanical plate and a modern historical review. For general readers interested in plants and the history of science, RN connects the history of a medicine with a practical question about evidence: what changes when a writer includes the cases that did not go well? Her contribution is source comparison, historical synthesis and explanatory writing. A seven-slide sequence, planned page-image crops, platform copy and filming scripts extend the essay; the package specifies no interactive component.
boundary: Drafted and held, with no verified publication URL. This is a research-based plant-history piece, not a report of RN visiting Pisa, conducting a clinical study or recommending a remedy. The source review covers selected pages of Withering's book, not all his case histories, and therefore does not establish a complete case count or outcomes. The early Welsh history and later medicine timeline rely on a modern review rather than direct reading of every underlying source. The draft excludes preparation instructions and amounts. Historical quotations, medical claims, image crops, licences and finished media have not been independently cleared in this intake. Planning dates, reshare timing and the chronology of the source checks remain inconsistent.
provenance: The complete manuscript, research log, dossier, filming notes, image-audit text and production-set text were reviewed, including all image metadata. title: Mystical Experience and Fear of Death: Said on Stage, Checked in the Paper
question: How do questionnaire scores, proportions of participants and different measures of attitudes toward death change the meaning of a research claim?
expression: RN's draft Polymath essay for Ask a Neuroscientist examines how two cancer-distress trials measured mystical-type experiences and attitudes toward death. It separates an average questionnaire score from a proportion of people, distinguishes death acceptance from death anxiety and death transcendence, and asks what a statistical mediation analysis can establish. RN's contribution is comparing research methods and translating their limits for general readers. The essay belongs to the proposed Said on Stage, Checked in the Paper series. An eight-slide sequence, chart and text-crop instructions, platform drafts and filming scripts support the same work. Related manuscripts discuss the same trials through broader cancer-distress evidence, comparisons across conditions and claims about harms; this essay concentrates on the measurements and the proposed link between experience and fear of death.
boundary: Drafted and held, with no verified publication URL. The conference quotation underlying the draft comes from a machine transcript that has not been checked against audio; that quotation is not reproduced here. The source package explicitly requires confirmation before posting. The trial discussion concerns small, selected groups, different scales and crossover designs; a statistical relationship is not proof of a mechanism. Scientific claims, quotation accuracy, supplementary evidence, image fidelity, licences and finished media have not been independently cleared in this intake. One platform draft blurs a treatment result with a correlation, and planning dates and source-check chronology disagree. RN did not conduct these trials. This is an explanatory essay draft, not clinical guidance, a treatment service or a completed film.

title: How Do You Know Where Your Hand Is With Your Eyes Closed? The Receptor Called PIEZO2
question: How do scientists connect a pressure-sensitive channel in a cell to the way people feel touch and know where their limbs are?
expression: RN's Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses the everyday experience of touching your nose with your eyes closed to explain research on PIEZO2. For general readers curious about sensation, she traces the discovery of mechanically activated channels, compares mouse studies of light touch and body position, and examines a two-patient human study alongside a later rare-condition case report. RN's contribution is research synthesis and explanatory writing, with attention to what each study can establish and how people compensate through other senses. A nine-slide receptor-card sequence, research notes, proposed charts, platform adaptations and a filming script support the same essay. This is separate from the existing PIEZO1 essay about blood flow and from the design-linked essays about pleasant touch and material perception.
boundary: Draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine, with no verified publication URL. The source's earlier abstract-only review notes are followed by a later full-paper review log; neither constitutes independent scientific clearance in this portfolio intake. The human studies are small, and the essay does not establish that one channel explains every aspect of touch, movement or balance. The everyday opening is an explanatory hook, not a diagnostic test. The manuscript and supporting posts differ in coverage and planning dates, and an inconsistent account of the discovery screen needs source attribution. Charts, molecular images, quotations, licences and finished media remain subject to review. RN did not conduct these studies, and the package does not establish a completed film, interview or delivered educational programme.

title: Names, Labels and the Brain
question: What can a music box that turns names into notes help readers ask about attention, sound and personal meaning?
expression: RN's Ask a Neuroscientist editorial package takes Iji Shin's Play the name installation as a starting point for explaining research on spoken names and sound. For general readers and designers, RN connects a study of brain responses to a person's own name with work on matching sounds to shapes and on synaesthesia, in which one kind of sensation is associated with another. The recovered material includes an eight-slide sequence, platform copy, a newsletter item, a maker spotlight, short-video scripts and a longer outline intended for Polymath and YouTube. The longer outline also considers music and autobiographical memory. RN's contribution is research synthesis, explanatory writing and editorial planning; the installation and its letter-to-note mechanism are the designer's work. The package keeps the central question open: findings about hearing a spoken name do not establish what happens when that name is encoded as a melody.

RN did not visit or record the installation, and the recovered materials do not establish a filmed interview, finished video, delivered installation or published article. Scientific claims, source quotations, image permissions and rendered media still require review. title: Same Birthday, Different Speeds: What the Dunedin Study Learned About the Pace of Aging
question: How do researchers measure the pace of aging, and what can a changing research marker tell us about health?
expression: RN's Ask a Neuroscientist essay explains how the Dunedin Study followed changes within a birth cohort and how later research developed a blood-based measure using chemical marks on DNA. Written for general readers interested in aging and scientific measurement, it compares the original repeated body measurements, the later methylation measure and a subsequent analysis of a randomized trial. RN's contribution is explanatory research synthesis: distinguishing measurement reliability, associations with health and changes in a trial, rather than presenting them as interchangeable evidence. Research notes, a six-slide sequence, platform adaptations and filming scripts support the draft. An existing coded slider illustrates how different example rates accumulate over twenty calendar years; its arithmetic and preset handlers received bounded checks, but it is not a personal aging test.
boundary: Unpublished draft intended for Polymath, with no verified reading destination. RN did not conduct the underlying studies or develop the research biomarker. The essay retains the development cohort's geographic limits, small and variable trial effects, observational associations and the distinction between a research marker and later illness or lifespan. It does not recommend calorie restriction, endorse a commercial test or estimate an individual's health. Some shorter adaptations blur the distinction between the earlier and later measures. Planning dates, figure licences, sample descriptions and image assignments still need reconciliation. Primary papers, finished media and rights have not been independently cleared in this portfolio review, and the slider has not received browser or accessibility acceptance.
provenance: The complete manuscript, research notes, dossier, filming brief and interactive source were reviewed in the preceding intake. title: What Does Grief Do to the Body?
question: What can research on bereavement explain about physical health after a loss, and where does that evidence stop?
expression: RN’s prepared Reader Q&A essay for Ask a Neuroscientist and Polymath answers a general reader’s question about grief and the body. It follows a review of bereavement research and a meta-analysis of widowhood and mortality, explaining how researchers study stress hormones, inflammation, immune responses, sleep and changing health risks. The manuscript distinguishes grief from bereavement, explains relative risk and follows different patterns of adjustment after a spouse dies. It also examines what studies measured before a loss, how caregiving and other circumstances can affect comparisons, and why group averages cannot describe every person. RN’s evidenced role is research synthesis and explanatory writing. The supporting package includes a six-slide sequence, platform adaptations, chart and figure plans, interview questions and short-video scripts. These are supporting forms of the same essay, not additional works or evidence of completed filming.
boundary: An unpublished draft in the current owner register, with no publication URL. Its evidence is chiefly about spouses and observational studies, so the essay does not establish a single biological mechanism, predict an individual’s health or automatically describe other kinds of loss. The source package contains conflicting time windows for a vaccine-response finding and needs reconciliation of some statistical, image and adaptation details. Its planning dates also differ across files. Source-owner fact-check and image-audit labels are not independent scientific or rights clearance. This portfolio review does not verify the cited primary studies, finished media, licences or a clinical recommendation. The essay and its adaptations remain held for editorial review.
provenance: The complete manuscript was reviewed in the preceding intake; its current revision was confirmed unchanged. title: Word of the Week: MAO Inhibitor
question: How can readers understand an enzyme inhibitor by connecting a glossary definition with the evidence used to describe a protein?
expression: RN’s Ask a Neuroscientist glossary explainer develops the fifth term from her original glossary carousel into a longer educational essay. For readers encountering neuroscience terminology, it moves from a short definition to the distinction between two forms of the enzyme, how researchers study its structure, and what an isolated protein model can and cannot show about a living brain. RN’s contribution is explanatory writing, research synthesis and the teaching sequence, not the underlying experiments. The package includes a six-slide sequence, source and claim notes, platform adaptations, interview questions, molecular-view and botanical-photo specifications, a short filming plan and a nine-chapter narrated-video script. These are supporting adaptations of one editorial work within Ask a Neuroscientist, rather than separate studies or completed publications.

title: Periods, Body Clocks and Work: What the Studies Show and Do Not Show
question: What can research on menstrual symptoms, cognitive tasks and daily rhythms tell readers about work, and which workplace questions remain unanswered?
expression: RN’s prepared Ask a Neuroscientist essay uses Juliana La Bella’s Beyond Linear Time installation as a starting point for a general reader’s guide to three different kinds of evidence. It separates a survey about symptoms and self-reported productivity, a study of hormones and cognitive tasks across menstrual cycles, and a small experiment on chronotype and time of day. RN’s contribution is the research synthesis, explanatory writing and editorial connection between those studies and workplace design; the installation is La Bella’s work. The manuscript explains selection bias, repeated testing and the limits of moving from laboratory tasks to real jobs. Supporting materials include a seven-slide sequence, platform copy, chart and diagram specifications, interview questions, short filming notes and a seven-chapter narrated-video script. An expanded Polymath draft explores disclosure, pain, period poverty and perspective-taking; its own handoff identifies it as an outline awaiting a later rewrite. These related drafts and adaptations stay together here, while the DDW project’s full content remains in its separate destination.
boundary: Unpublished draft intended for Fat Nugs Magazine, with supporting Polymath material. The current owner register has no publication link. title: The Room Where Galileo Was Sentenced: The Convent of the Minerva
question: How can a place-based history explain Galileo's trial while showing readers where the surviving account remains incomplete?
expression: RN's draft for Polymath follows Galileo's 1633 abjuration at the Dominican convent beside Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome. Written for general readers interested in the history of science and the places where it happened, it compares museum accounts of the book, summons, sentence and later confinement with a Ministry of Culture account of the building. RN's contribution is documentary comparison and explanatory writing: the essay preserves two different summons dates instead of inventing a reconciliation and separates what its sources describe from what they leave unknown. A six-slide sequence, platform adaptations, historical-image and chart plans, short filming scripts and a five-chapter narrated-video script support the same work.
